1	# App Configuration
2	
3	`AppBuilder` is the unified entry point for configuring your application. Instead of scattering configuration across multiple structs (`Standout`, `RenderSetup`, `Theme`), everything from command registration to theme selection happens in one fluent interface.
4	
5	This design ensures that your application defines its entire environment—commands, styles, templates, and hooks—before the runtime starts, preventing configuration race conditions and simplifying testing.
6	
7	This guide covers the full setup: embedding resources, registering commands, configuring themes, and customizing behavior.
8	
9	See also:
10	
11	- [Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md) and [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) for templates and styles.
12	- [Topics System](topics-system.md) for help topics.
13	
14	## Basic Setup
15	
16	```rust
17	use standout::cli::{App, FnHandler};
18	use standout_macros::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
19	
20	let app = App::builder()
21	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
22	    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
23	    .default_theme("default")
24	    .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |config| config.template_name("list"))?
25	    .build()?;
26	
27	app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
28	```
29	
30	## Embedding Resources
31	
32	### Templates
33	
34	`embed_templates!` embeds template files at compile time:
35	
36	```rust
37	.templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
38	```
39	
40	Collects files matching: `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt` (in priority order).
41	
42	> **Custom template engines:** For advanced use cases, `standout-render` supports pluggable template engines. See the [Template Engines](../crates/render/topics/template-engines.md) topic for details on using `SimpleEngine` or implementing custom engines.
43	
44	Directory structure:
45	
46	```text
47	src/templates/
48	  list.j2
49	  add.j2
50	  db/
51	    migrate.j2
52	    status.j2
53	```
54	
55	Templates are referenced by path without extension: `"list"`, `"db/migrate"`.
56	
57	### Styles
58	
59	`embed_styles!` embeds stylesheet files:
60	
61	```rust
62	.styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
63	```
64	
65	Collects files matching: `.css` (and legacy `.yaml`, `.yml`).
66	
67	```text
68	src/styles/
69	  default.css
70	  dark.css
71	  light.css
72	```
73	
74	Themes are referenced by filename without extension: `"default"`, `"dark"`.
75	
76	### Hot Reloading
77	
78	In debug builds, embedded resources are re-read from disk on each render—edit without recompiling. In release builds, embedded content is used directly.
79	
80	This is automatic when the source path exists on disk.
81	
82	## Resources Read at Run Time
83	
84	`templates_dir` and `styles_dir` add a directory read at run time, for
85	resources that live outside the crate source tree and so cannot be embedded:
86	
87	```rust
88	App::builder()
89	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
90	    .templates_dir("~/.myapp/templates")  // Adds names the binary does not embed
91	    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
92	    .styles_dir("~/.myapp/themes")        // Likewise for themes
93	```
94	
95	These directories **add** names; they do not replace them. A registry resolves
96	an embedded name before it looks at any directory registered this way, so a
97	`~/.myapp/templates/list.jinja` sitting beside an embedded `list` never
98	renders — see [Resolution Priority](../crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md#resolution-priority).
99	To let a user directory win, register only the directory, without the
100	`embed_templates!` call, when that directory exists.
101	
102	## Theme Selection
103	
104	### From Stylesheet Registry
105	
106	```rust
107	    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
108	    .default_theme("dark")
109	```
110	
111	`.default_theme(name)` names the theme `build()` loads from the stylesheet
112	registry; if that name isn't found, `build()` returns
113	`SetupError::ThemeNotFound`. With no `.default_theme(...)` call, `build()`
114	does not fall back to any conventional name — the application resolves to no
115	application theme, leaving the framework's own base styling.
116	
117	### Explicit Theme
118	
119	```rust
120	let theme = Theme::new()
121	    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
122	    .add("muted", Style::new().dim());
123	
124	App::builder()
125	    .theme(theme)
126	```
127	
128	`.theme(...)` sets the theme directly, bypassing the stylesheet registry.
129	Calling both `.styles(...)` and `.theme(...)` on the same builder is a
130	`SetupError` that names both calls — configure one path or the other, not
131	both.
132	
133	## Command Registration
134	
135	### Simple Commands
136	
137	```rust
138	App::builder()
139	    .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
140	    .command_with("add", FnHandler::new(add_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
141	```
142	
143	`AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, not a bare function, so a
144	plain `fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>` is wrapped in
145	`FnHandler::new(...)` first; a `#[handler]`-annotated function registers as the
146	`name_Handler` struct the macro generates instead. (`GroupBuilder::command_with`
147	— the entry `.commands(...)` and `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reach — takes the bare
148	closure and wraps it for you, which is why the nested-group example below does
149	not name `FnHandler`.)
150	
151	With no `.template_name(...)` set on the `CommandConfig`, the template
152	resolves by convention: the command path with `.` replaced by `/` (`list`,
153	`add`), matched against the registered templates using the extension list
154	`.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`.
155	
156	### With Configuration
157	
158	```rust
159	App::builder()
160	    .command_with("delete", FnHandler::new(delete_handler), |cfg| cfg
161	        .template_name("delete")
162	        .pre_dispatch(require_confirmation)
163	        .post_dispatch(log_deletion))?
164	```
165	
166	Inline command configuration can also attach a
167	`StructuredOutputProjection` for CSV shaping. The projection stays at the
168	presentation boundary: it sees post-dispatch data, and handlers remain
169	independent of the selected output mode. See [Output Modes](output-modes.md#csv-output).
170	
171	### Nested Groups
172	
173	```rust
174	App::builder()
175	    .commands(|g| g
176	        .group("db", |g| g
177	            .command("migrate", migrate_handler)
178	            .command("status", status_handler)
179	            .group("backup", |b| b
180	                .command("create", backup_create)
181	                .command("restore", backup_restore))))?
182	```
183	
184	Creates command paths: `db.migrate`, `db.status`, `db.backup.create`,
185	`db.backup.restore`. Each resolves, by convention, to a template named after
186	its path (`db/migrate`, `db/status`, `db/backup/create`,
187	`db/backup/restore`); attach a `CommandConfig` to a group entry with
188	`command_with` instead of `command` when one needs `.template_name(...)` or
189	another `CommandConfig` setting.
190	
191	### From Dispatch Macro
192	
193	```rust
194	#[derive(Dispatch)]
195	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
196	enum Commands {
197	    List,
198	    Add,
199	    #[dispatch(nested)]
200	    Db(DbCommands),
201	}
202	
203	App::builder()
204	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
205	```
206	
207	`#[dispatch(handlers = <module path>)]` on the enum is required: it names the
208	module `Dispatch` looks up each variant's handler function in (`handlers::list`
209	for `List`, `handlers::add` for `Add`). A nested variant's own type
210	(`DbCommands` here) needs its own `#[derive(Dispatch)]` with its own
211	`#[dispatch(handlers = ...)]` — the macro generates registration for all
212	variants, but a container attribute is scoped to the enum it's on.
213	
214	## Default Command
215	
216	When a CLI is invoked without a subcommand (a "naked" invocation like `myapp` or `myapp --verbose`), you can specify a default command to run:
217	
218	```rust
219	App::builder()
220	    .default_command("list")
221	    .command("list", list_handler, "{{ items | length }} items")
222	    .command("add", add_handler, "Added {{ name }}")
223	```
224	
225	With this configuration:
226	
227	- `myapp` becomes `myapp list`
228	- `myapp --output=json` becomes `myapp list --output=json`
229	- `myapp add foo` stays as `myapp add foo` (explicit command takes precedence)
230	
231	Default resolution applies to both the integrated dispatch path (`run`, `run_with`) and configured parsing (`get_matches_from`). If you parse first and build dispatch state afterwards, the matches you get back already name the resolved command.
232	
233	### Invocation-Aware Defaults
234	
235	A fixed name can't express "it depends". `default_command_with` chooses the default per invocation:
236	
237	```rust
238	App::builder()
239	    .default_command_with(|ctx| {
240	        Some(if ctx.stdin_is_piped() { "add" } else { "list" }.to_string())
241	    })
242	    .command("list", list_handler, "{{ items | length }} items")
243	    .command("add", add_handler, "Added {{ name }}")
244	```
245	
246	- `myapp` at a terminal becomes `myapp list`
247	- `cat notes.txt | myapp` becomes `myapp add`, which reads the pipe
248	- `myapp done 3` stays as `myapp done 3`
249	
250	The resolver receives a `DefaultCommandContext` exposing only the facts needed to pick a command:
251	
252	| Method | Fact |
253	| --- | --- |
254	| `matches()` | The parsed root `ArgMatches` — globals and root flags |
255	| `app_state::<T>()` | Read-only app state registered via `.app_state(...)` |
256	| `stdin_is_terminal()` / `stdin_is_piped()` | Whether stdin is redirected |
257	
258	Plus `std::env` for env-derived facts. The matches are the root's, so global flags and root arguments are all there; there is no subcommand, because that is what makes the invocation naked.
259	
260	**Stdin is never read during resolution.** The terminal check is the same non-consuming `StdinReader::is_terminal` seam the input system uses, so a handler's `InputChain` still consumes the pipe normally afterwards. This also means piped-but-empty stdin is a *pipe*, not a terminal — emptiness is only knowable by reading, which resolution never does. If empty input should be an error, that's the receiving command's `InputChain` policy, not the resolver's.
261	
262	### Ordering guarantees
263	
264	**Clap decides which command a line named**, and resolution reads that decision. A parse that selected a subcommand is not naked; a parse that selected none is.
265	
266	- **Explicit and nested commands** short-circuit resolution — the resolver never runs.
267	- **`--help` / `--version`** are Clap's own displays: no default is inserted, so `myapp --help` renders the root's help rather than a default command's.
268	- **Invalid syntax** stays a Clap usage error (exit 2). If a default command is configured, a refused line is offered to it — `myapp --all` is a naked line at a root that has no `--all`, and becomes `myapp list --all` when `--all` belongs to `list` — and whatever the amended line parses to, success or failure, is what you get.
269	- **`--`**, option values, aliases, and short clusters mean exactly what they mean everywhere else, because the same parser reads them.
270	
271	A root that requires a subcommand — what `#[command(subcommand)] command: Commands` produces — still accepts a naked invocation: the line is refused, the default is substituted, and the amended line parses. The field does not have to be `Option<Commands>`. See [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).
272	
273	### Combining both
274	
275	Both may be configured together. The resolver is consulted first; returning `None` declines to the static default:
276	
277	```rust
278	App::builder()
279	    // Pipes mean `add`; everything else falls back to `list`.
280	    .default_command("list")
281	    .default_command_with(|ctx| ctx.stdin_is_piped().then(|| "add".to_string()))
282	```
283	
284	Returning a name that isn't a command of your `clap::Command` fails the run with `RunErrorKind::DefaultCommand` (exit 1), carrying a diagnostic that names the offending resolver output and lists the valid commands. A resolver naming a command the CLI doesn't have is an application bug, so it's reported as one rather than reaching Clap as a usage error blaming the user. Return `None` to decline.
285	
286	Validation is against your `clap::Command`'s names, not Standout's registered handlers — so partial adoption stays coherent: resolving to a Clap command Standout doesn't handle yields `NoMatch`, exactly as typing it explicitly would.
287	
288	### With Dispatch Macro
289	
290	Use the `#[dispatch(default)]` attribute to mark a variant as the default:
291	
292	```rust
293	#[derive(Dispatch)]
294	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
295	enum Commands {
296	    #[dispatch(default)]
297	    List,
298	    Add,
299	}
300	
301	App::builder()
302	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
303	```
304	
305	Only one command can be marked as default. Multiple `#[dispatch(default)]` attributes will cause a compile error.
306	
307	## Hooks
308	
309	Attach hooks to specific command paths:
310	
311	```rust
312	App::builder()
313	    .command_with("db.migrate", FnHandler::new(migrate_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
314	    .hooks("db.migrate", Hooks::new()
315	        .pre_dispatch(require_admin)
316	        .post_dispatch(add_timestamp)
317	        .post_output(log_result))
318	```
319	
320	The path uses dot notation matching the command hierarchy.
321	
322	### Hook order, and where a questionnaire sits in it
323	
324	Pre-dispatch hooks run in the order they were registered — `Hooks` keeps them
325	in a list and `run_pre_dispatch` walks it front to back. The same holds for
326	post-dispatch and post-output.
327	
328	`CommandConfig::questionnaire::<T>()` is a pre-dispatch hook, so it takes its
329	place in that same order: a `.pre_dispatch(f)` written *before* it runs before
330	the answers are resolved and cannot read them, and one written *after* it runs
331	with `ctx.questionnaire::<T>()` already populated.
332	
333	```rust,ignore
334	// `check_permissions` runs first, then the questionnaire resolves,
335	// then `audit` runs and can read the answers.
336	CommandConfig::new(handler)
337	    .pre_dispatch(check_permissions)
338	    .questionnaire::<ProvisionAnswers>()
339	    .pre_dispatch(audit)
340	```
341	
342	One trap goes with that: `CommandConfig::hooks(hooks)` *replaces* the config's
343	hook set rather than appending to it, so calling `.hooks(…)` after
344	`.questionnaire::<T>()` discards the questionnaire's own hook and the answers
345	never resolve. Register per-phase with `.pre_dispatch(…)` when a questionnaire
346	is involved.
347	
348	Registering the same phase for one path through both `CommandConfig` and
349	`AppBuilder::hooks` is a configuration error naming the path and the phase,
350	rather than one hook set silently replacing the other.
351	
352	> Stating a single ordering rule for pre-dispatch hooks — including which
353	> matches they receive — is issue #352 in the adopter-seams epic. What is
354	> written above is today's behavior.
355	
356	## Context Injection
357	
358	Add values available in all templates:
359	
360	### Static Context
361	
362	```rust
363	App::builder()
364	    .context("version", "1.0.0")
365	    .context("app_name", "MyApp")
366	```
367	
368	### Dynamic Context
369	
370	```rust
371	App::builder()
372	    .context_fn("terminal_width", |ctx| {
373	        Value::from(ctx.terminal_width.unwrap_or(80))
374	    })
375	    .context_fn("timestamp", |_ctx| {
376	        Value::from(chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339())
377	    })
378	```
379	
380	Dynamic providers receive `RenderContext` with output mode, terminal width, and handler data.
381	They also receive `ctx.ambiguous_width()`, the application's explicit
382	East Asian Ambiguous character-width policy. Configure it at the rendering
383	seam; narrow is the compatibility default and Standout does not infer a locale:
384	
385	```rust
386	use standout::{AmbiguousWidth, cli::App};
387	
388	let app = App::builder()
389	    .ambiguous_width(AmbiguousWidth::Wide)
390	    .build()?;
391	```
392	
393	## Topics
394	
395	Add help topics:
396	
397	```rust
398	App::builder()
399	    .topics_dir("docs/topics")
400	    .add_topic(Topic::new("auth", "Authentication...", TopicType::Text, None))
401	```
402	
403	See [Topics System](topics-system.md) for details.
404	
405	## Version
406	
407	Application version metadata belongs on the builder, next to the rest of the
408	app's configuration:
409	
410	```rust
411	App::builder()
412	    .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
413	```
414	
415	Standout applies the value to the root command wherever it augments and parses
416	it, so every entry point — `run`, `run_with`, `get_matches_from`, and
417	`TestHarness` — answers `myapp --version` the same way:
418	Clap's own display, on stdout, exit status 0, typed as
419	`SuccessKind::ClapVersion` (see [Execution
420	Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md)).
421	
422	Clap keeps owning the spelling and formatting of that output and the display
423	short-circuit; the builder only says what the version is. Leave `.version()`
424	unset and the supplied `clap::Command` is untouched, including a version
425	configured on Clap directly.
426	
427	This is separate from `.context("version", …)`, which puts a value in *templates*
428	(`{{ version }}`); an app that wants both says both.
429	
430	## Flag Customization
431	
432	### Output Flag
433	
434	```rust
435	App::builder()
436	    .output_flag(Some("format"))  // --format instead of --output
437	```
438	
439	```rust
440	App::builder()
441	    .no_output_flag()  // Disable entirely
442	```
443	
444	### Output Mode Fallback
445	
446	The mode used when the flag is absent from the command line. It defaults to
447	`OutputMode::Auto`; an application that decides its own default — from its own
448	environment variable, a config file, or anything else it reads at build time —
449	sets it here:
450	
451	```rust
452	App::builder()
453	    .output_mode_fallback(OutputMode::Term)
454	```
455	
456	Precedence is `--output` first, then the fallback. An explicit `--output` always
457	wins, so this sets the default rather than overriding the user. Forcing color
458	regardless of mode is a separate axis and is not what this call does.
459	
460	Every path that renders without an `--output` on the command line uses the
461	fallback: command output, both help spellings (`app help` and `app --help`), the
462	`--output` help entry's advertised default, and the diagnostics of errors raised
463	before parsing. `app --help` renders in the fallback even when the command line
464	does carry an `--output` — the help flags never read the flag ([Help](./standout-help.md#output-modes)).
465	
466	### File Output Flag
467	
468	```rust
469	App::builder()
470	    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))  // --out instead of --output-file-path
471	```
472	
473	```rust
474	App::builder()
475	    .no_output_file_flag()  // Disable entirely
476	```
477	
478	## The App Struct
479	
480	`build()` produces an `App`. The theme `build()` merged is always present
481	(`theme: Theme`); `get_default_theme()` returns `&Theme`.
482	
483	```rust
484	pub struct App {
485	    registry: TopicRegistry,
486	    output_flag: Option<String>,
487	    output_mode_fallback: OutputMode,
488	    output_file_flag: Option<String>,
489	    theme: Theme,
490	    command_hooks: HashMap<String, Hooks>,
491	    template_registry: Option<TemplateRegistry>,
492	    stylesheet_registry: Option<StylesheetRegistry>,
493	}
494	```
495	
496	## Running the App
497	
498	### Standard Execution
499	
500	```rust
501	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
502	    // Standout did not handle this command; fall back to legacy dispatch.
503	    legacy_dispatch();
504	}
505	```
506	
507	Parses args, dispatches to a handler, and performs the final write. It returns
508	`true` when Standout handled the command and `false` for an unmatched fallback.
509	Help/version and successes use stdout/status 0, usage errors use stderr/status
510	2, and runtime/write failures use stderr/status 1. The two owner-declared
511	failures are the exceptions: `AppFailure` carries the application's own nonzero
512	status and verbatim stderr payload, and `ExternalFailure` preserves an
513	authoritative external operation's. See [Error Handling](./error-handling.md).
514	
515	### Capture Output
516	
517	For tests, reach for `standout_test::TestHarness` (see [Testing](./testing.md)).
518	For post-processing, or any other embedding caller that needs the output
519	string, pass destination properties and input sources in explicitly:
520	
521	```rust
522	let target = TargetProperties::detect();
523	let sources = InputSources::from_process();
524	let result = app.run_with(cmd, args, target, sources);
525	let _ = result.warnings();
526	match result.into_outcome() {
527	    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => { /* use output string */ }
528	    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => { /* handle binary */ }
529	    DispatchResult::Error(error) => { /* inspect error.kind() */ }
530	    DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches) => { /* fallback dispatch */ }
531	    _ => {}
532	}
533	```
534	
535	Returns `CompletedRun` instead of printing: a wrapper around `DispatchResult`
536	plus framework warnings. Use `exit_status()`, `success_kind()`, and
537	`error_kind()` for typed assertions; see [Execution
538	Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md).
539	
540	### Parse Only
541	
542	```rust
543	match app.get_matches_from(cmd, std::env::args(), &InputSources::from_process()) {
544	    HelpResult::Matches(matches) => { /* use matches for manual dispatch */ }
545	    HelpResult::Help(text) | HelpResult::PagedHelp(text) => { /* the invocation asked for help */ }
546	    HelpResult::Error(e) => { /* a clap::Error: usage failure, or --version display */ }
547	}
548	```
549	
550	Parses with Standout's augmented command, intercepting help display; returns
551	matches only when the invocation didn't trigger a help/usage/version display.
552	
553	## Build Validation
554	
555	`build()` validates:
556	
557	- a theme registry exists and contains the theme named by `.default_theme(...)`
558	- named templates resolve through `.templates(...)` or `.templates_dir(...)`
559	- convention templates resolve when application templates are configured; without application templates, human-mode rendering reports the missing convention template at runtime
560	- registered templates compile
561	- framework templates only use tags defined by the resolved theme
562	- `command_groups`, topics, and `help_word(true)` are not combined with `.help_handling(false)`
563	- commands do not collide with the `help` word standout installs when help handling is on
564	- the same command path and hook phase are not configured through both `CommandConfig` and `AppBuilder::hooks`
565	
566	What's NOT validated at build time:
567	
568	- Command handlers
569	- Hook signatures (verified at registration)
570	
571	## Complete Example
572	
573	```rust
574	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, FnHandler, HandlerResult, Output};
575	use standout_macros::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
576	use clap::{Command, ArgMatches};
577	use serde::Serialize;
578	
579	#[derive(Serialize)]
580	struct ListOutput {
581	    items: Vec<String>,
582	}
583	
584	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
585	    let items = vec!["one".into(), "two".into()];
586	    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items }))
587	}
588	
589	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
590	    let cli = Command::new("myapp")
591	        .subcommand(Command::new("list").about("List items"));
592	
593	    let app = App::builder()
594	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
595	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
596	        .default_theme("default")
597	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
598	        .context("version", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").into())
599	        .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |config| {
600	            config.template_name("list")
601	        })?
602	        .topics_dir("docs/topics")?
603	        .build()?;
604	
605	    app.run(cli, std::env::args());
606	    Ok(())
607	}
608	```
609	
610	Template `src/templates/list.j2`:
611	
612	```jinja
613	[header]Items[/header] ({{ items | length }} total)
614	{% for item in items %}
615	  - {{ item }}
616	{% endfor %}
617	
618	[muted]v{{ version }}[/muted]
619	```
620	
621	Style `src/styles/default.css`:
622	
623	```css
624	.header { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
625	.muted { opacity: 0.5; }
626	```

# App Configuration

`AppBuilder` is the unified entry point for configuring your application. Instead of scattering configuration across multiple structs (`Standout`, `RenderSetup`, `Theme`), everything from command registration to theme selection happens in one fluent interface.

This design ensures that your application defines its entire environment—commands, styles, templates, and hooks—before the runtime starts, preventing configuration race conditions and simplifying testing.

This guide covers the full setup: embedding resources, registering commands, configuring themes, and customizing behavior.

See also:

- [Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md) and [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) for templates and styles.
- [Topics System](topics-system.md) for help topics.

## Basic Setup

```rust
use standout::cli::{App, FnHandler};
use standout_macros::{embed_templates, embed_styles};

let app = App::builder()
    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
    .default_theme("default")
    .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |config| config.template_name("list"))?
    .build()?;

app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
```

## Embedding Resources

### Templates

`embed_templates!` embeds template files at compile time:

```rust
.templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
```

Collects files matching: `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt` (in priority order).

> **Custom template engines:** For advanced use cases, `standout-render` supports pluggable template engines. See the [Template Engines](../crates/render/topics/template-engines.md) topic for details on using `SimpleEngine` or implementing custom engines.

Directory structure:

```text
src/templates/
  list.j2
  add.j2
  db/
    migrate.j2
    status.j2
```

Templates are referenced by path without extension: `"list"`, `"db/migrate"`.

### Styles

`embed_styles!` embeds stylesheet files:

```rust
.styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
```

Collects files matching: `.css` (and legacy `.yaml`, `.yml`).

```text
src/styles/
  default.css
  dark.css
  light.css
```

Themes are referenced by filename without extension: `"default"`, `"dark"`.

### Hot Reloading

In debug builds, embedded resources are re-read from disk on each render—edit without recompiling. In release builds, embedded content is used directly.

This is automatic when the source path exists on disk.

## Resources Read at Run Time

`templates_dir` and `styles_dir` add a directory read at run time, for
resources that live outside the crate source tree and so cannot be embedded:

```rust
App::builder()
    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
    .templates_dir("~/.myapp/templates")  // Adds names the binary does not embed
    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
    .styles_dir("~/.myapp/themes")        // Likewise for themes
```

These directories **add** names; they do not replace them. A registry resolves
an embedded name before it looks at any directory registered this way, so a
`~/.myapp/templates/list.jinja` sitting beside an embedded `list` never
renders — see [Resolution Priority](../crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md#resolution-priority).
To let a user directory win, register only the directory, without the
`embed_templates!` call, when that directory exists.

## Theme Selection

### From Stylesheet Registry

```rust
    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
    .default_theme("dark")
```

`.default_theme(name)` names the theme `build()` loads from the stylesheet
registry; if that name isn't found, `build()` returns
`SetupError::ThemeNotFound`. With no `.default_theme(...)` call, `build()`
does not fall back to any conventional name — the application resolves to no
application theme, leaving the framework's own base styling.

### Explicit Theme

```rust
let theme = Theme::new()
    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
    .add("muted", Style::new().dim());

App::builder()
    .theme(theme)
```

`.theme(...)` sets the theme directly, bypassing the stylesheet registry.
Calling both `.styles(...)` and `.theme(...)` on the same builder is a
`SetupError` that names both calls — configure one path or the other, not
both.

## Command Registration

### Simple Commands

```rust
App::builder()
    .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
    .command_with("add", FnHandler::new(add_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
```

`AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, not a bare function, so a
plain `fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>` is wrapped in
`FnHandler::new(...)` first; a `#[handler]`-annotated function registers as the
`name_Handler` struct the macro generates instead. (`GroupBuilder::command_with`
— the entry `.commands(...)` and `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reach — takes the bare
closure and wraps it for you, which is why the nested-group example below does
not name `FnHandler`.)

With no `.template_name(...)` set on the `CommandConfig`, the template
resolves by convention: the command path with `.` replaced by `/` (`list`,
`add`), matched against the registered templates using the extension list
`.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`.

### With Configuration

```rust
App::builder()
    .command_with("delete", FnHandler::new(delete_handler), |cfg| cfg
        .template_name("delete")
        .pre_dispatch(require_confirmation)
        .post_dispatch(log_deletion))?
```

Inline command configuration can also attach a
`StructuredOutputProjection` for CSV shaping. The projection stays at the
presentation boundary: it sees post-dispatch data, and handlers remain
independent of the selected output mode. See [Output Modes](output-modes.md#csv-output).

### Nested Groups

```rust
App::builder()
    .commands(|g| g
        .group("db", |g| g
            .command("migrate", migrate_handler)
            .command("status", status_handler)
            .group("backup", |b| b
                .command("create", backup_create)
                .command("restore", backup_restore))))?
```

Creates command paths: `db.migrate`, `db.status`, `db.backup.create`,
`db.backup.restore`. Each resolves, by convention, to a template named after
its path (`db/migrate`, `db/status`, `db/backup/create`,
`db/backup/restore`); attach a `CommandConfig` to a group entry with
`command_with` instead of `command` when one needs `.template_name(...)` or
another `CommandConfig` setting.

### From Dispatch Macro

```rust
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    List,
    Add,
    #[dispatch(nested)]
    Db(DbCommands),
}

App::builder()
    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
```

`#[dispatch(handlers = <module path>)]` on the enum is required: it names the
module `Dispatch` looks up each variant's handler function in (`handlers::list`
for `List`, `handlers::add` for `Add`). A nested variant's own type
(`DbCommands` here) needs its own `#[derive(Dispatch)]` with its own
`#[dispatch(handlers = ...)]` — the macro generates registration for all
variants, but a container attribute is scoped to the enum it's on.

## Default Command

When a CLI is invoked without a subcommand (a "naked" invocation like `myapp` or `myapp --verbose`), you can specify a default command to run:

```rust
App::builder()
    .default_command("list")
    .command("list", list_handler, "{{ items | length }} items")
    .command("add", add_handler, "Added {{ name }}")
```

With this configuration:

- `myapp` becomes `myapp list`
- `myapp --output=json` becomes `myapp list --output=json`
- `myapp add foo` stays as `myapp add foo` (explicit command takes precedence)

Default resolution applies to both the integrated dispatch path (`run`, `run_with`) and configured parsing (`get_matches_from`). If you parse first and build dispatch state afterwards, the matches you get back already name the resolved command.

### Invocation-Aware Defaults

A fixed name can't express "it depends". `default_command_with` chooses the default per invocation:

```rust
App::builder()
    .default_command_with(|ctx| {
        Some(if ctx.stdin_is_piped() { "add" } else { "list" }.to_string())
    })
    .command("list", list_handler, "{{ items | length }} items")
    .command("add", add_handler, "Added {{ name }}")
```

- `myapp` at a terminal becomes `myapp list`
- `cat notes.txt | myapp` becomes `myapp add`, which reads the pipe
- `myapp done 3` stays as `myapp done 3`

The resolver receives a `DefaultCommandContext` exposing only the facts needed to pick a command:

| Method | Fact |
| --- | --- |
| `matches()` | The parsed root `ArgMatches` — globals and root flags |
| `app_state::<T>()` | Read-only app state registered via `.app_state(...)` |
| `stdin_is_terminal()` / `stdin_is_piped()` | Whether stdin is redirected |

Plus `std::env` for env-derived facts. The matches are the root's, so global flags and root arguments are all there; there is no subcommand, because that is what makes the invocation naked.

**Stdin is never read during resolution.** The terminal check is the same non-consuming `StdinReader::is_terminal` seam the input system uses, so a handler's `InputChain` still consumes the pipe normally afterwards. This also means piped-but-empty stdin is a *pipe*, not a terminal — emptiness is only knowable by reading, which resolution never does. If empty input should be an error, that's the receiving command's `InputChain` policy, not the resolver's.

### Ordering guarantees

**Clap decides which command a line named**, and resolution reads that decision. A parse that selected a subcommand is not naked; a parse that selected none is.

- **Explicit and nested commands** short-circuit resolution — the resolver never runs.
- **`--help` / `--version`** are Clap's own displays: no default is inserted, so `myapp --help` renders the root's help rather than a default command's.
- **Invalid syntax** stays a Clap usage error (exit 2). If a default command is configured, a refused line is offered to it — `myapp --all` is a naked line at a root that has no `--all`, and becomes `myapp list --all` when `--all` belongs to `list` — and whatever the amended line parses to, success or failure, is what you get.
- **`--`**, option values, aliases, and short clusters mean exactly what they mean everywhere else, because the same parser reads them.

A root that requires a subcommand — what `#[command(subcommand)] command: Commands` produces — still accepts a naked invocation: the line is refused, the default is substituted, and the amended line parses. The field does not have to be `Option<Commands>`. See [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).

### Combining both

Both may be configured together. The resolver is consulted first; returning `None` declines to the static default:

```rust
App::builder()
    // Pipes mean `add`; everything else falls back to `list`.
    .default_command("list")
    .default_command_with(|ctx| ctx.stdin_is_piped().then(|| "add".to_string()))
```

Returning a name that isn't a command of your `clap::Command` fails the run with `RunErrorKind::DefaultCommand` (exit 1), carrying a diagnostic that names the offending resolver output and lists the valid commands. A resolver naming a command the CLI doesn't have is an application bug, so it's reported as one rather than reaching Clap as a usage error blaming the user. Return `None` to decline.

Validation is against your `clap::Command`'s names, not Standout's registered handlers — so partial adoption stays coherent: resolving to a Clap command Standout doesn't handle yields `NoMatch`, exactly as typing it explicitly would.

### With Dispatch Macro

Use the `#[dispatch(default)]` attribute to mark a variant as the default:

```rust
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(default)]
    List,
    Add,
}

App::builder()
    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
```

Only one command can be marked as default. Multiple `#[dispatch(default)]` attributes will cause a compile error.

## Hooks

Attach hooks to specific command paths:

```rust
App::builder()
    .command_with("db.migrate", FnHandler::new(migrate_handler), |cfg| cfg)?
    .hooks("db.migrate", Hooks::new()
        .pre_dispatch(require_admin)
        .post_dispatch(add_timestamp)
        .post_output(log_result))
```

The path uses dot notation matching the command hierarchy.

### Hook order, and where a questionnaire sits in it

Pre-dispatch hooks run in the order they were registered — `Hooks` keeps them
in a list and `run_pre_dispatch` walks it front to back. The same holds for
post-dispatch and post-output.

`CommandConfig::questionnaire::<T>()` is a pre-dispatch hook, so it takes its
place in that same order: a `.pre_dispatch(f)` written *before* it runs before
the answers are resolved and cannot read them, and one written *after* it runs
with `ctx.questionnaire::<T>()` already populated.

```rust,ignore
// `check_permissions` runs first, then the questionnaire resolves,
// then `audit` runs and can read the answers.
CommandConfig::new(handler)
    .pre_dispatch(check_permissions)
    .questionnaire::<ProvisionAnswers>()
    .pre_dispatch(audit)
```

One trap goes with that: `CommandConfig::hooks(hooks)` *replaces* the config's
hook set rather than appending to it, so calling `.hooks(…)` after
`.questionnaire::<T>()` discards the questionnaire's own hook and the answers
never resolve. Register per-phase with `.pre_dispatch(…)` when a questionnaire
is involved.

Registering the same phase for one path through both `CommandConfig` and
`AppBuilder::hooks` is a configuration error naming the path and the phase,
rather than one hook set silently replacing the other.

> Stating a single ordering rule for pre-dispatch hooks — including which
> matches they receive — is issue #352 in the adopter-seams epic. What is
> written above is today's behavior.

## Context Injection

Add values available in all templates:

### Static Context

```rust
App::builder()
    .context("version", "1.0.0")
    .context("app_name", "MyApp")
```

### Dynamic Context

```rust
App::builder()
    .context_fn("terminal_width", |ctx| {
        Value::from(ctx.terminal_width.unwrap_or(80))
    })
    .context_fn("timestamp", |_ctx| {
        Value::from(chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339())
    })
```

Dynamic providers receive `RenderContext` with output mode, terminal width, and handler data.
They also receive `ctx.ambiguous_width()`, the application's explicit
East Asian Ambiguous character-width policy. Configure it at the rendering
seam; narrow is the compatibility default and Standout does not infer a locale:

```rust
use standout::{AmbiguousWidth, cli::App};

let app = App::builder()
    .ambiguous_width(AmbiguousWidth::Wide)
    .build()?;
```

## Topics

Add help topics:

```rust
App::builder()
    .topics_dir("docs/topics")
    .add_topic(Topic::new("auth", "Authentication...", TopicType::Text, None))
```

See [Topics System](topics-system.md) for details.

## Version

Application version metadata belongs on the builder, next to the rest of the
app's configuration:

```rust
App::builder()
    .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
```

Standout applies the value to the root command wherever it augments and parses
it, so every entry point — `run`, `run_with`, `get_matches_from`, and
`TestHarness` — answers `myapp --version` the same way:
Clap's own display, on stdout, exit status 0, typed as
`SuccessKind::ClapVersion` (see [Execution
Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md)).

Clap keeps owning the spelling and formatting of that output and the display
short-circuit; the builder only says what the version is. Leave `.version()`
unset and the supplied `clap::Command` is untouched, including a version
configured on Clap directly.

This is separate from `.context("version", …)`, which puts a value in *templates*
(`{{ version }}`); an app that wants both says both.

## Flag Customization

### Output Flag

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_flag(Some("format"))  // --format instead of --output
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_flag()  // Disable entirely
```

### Output Mode Fallback

The mode used when the flag is absent from the command line. It defaults to
`OutputMode::Auto`; an application that decides its own default — from its own
environment variable, a config file, or anything else it reads at build time —
sets it here:

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_mode_fallback(OutputMode::Term)
```

Precedence is `--output` first, then the fallback. An explicit `--output` always
wins, so this sets the default rather than overriding the user. Forcing color
regardless of mode is a separate axis and is not what this call does.

Every path that renders without an `--output` on the command line uses the
fallback: command output, both help spellings (`app help` and `app --help`), the
`--output` help entry's advertised default, and the diagnostics of errors raised
before parsing. `app --help` renders in the fallback even when the command line
does carry an `--output` — the help flags never read the flag ([Help](./standout-help.md#output-modes)).

### File Output Flag

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))  // --out instead of --output-file-path
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_file_flag()  // Disable entirely
```

## The App Struct

`build()` produces an `App`. The theme `build()` merged is always present
(`theme: Theme`); `get_default_theme()` returns `&Theme`.

```rust
pub struct App {
    registry: TopicRegistry,
    output_flag: Option<String>,
    output_mode_fallback: OutputMode,
    output_file_flag: Option<String>,
    theme: Theme,
    command_hooks: HashMap<String, Hooks>,
    template_registry: Option<TemplateRegistry>,
    stylesheet_registry: Option<StylesheetRegistry>,
}
```

## Running the App

### Standard Execution

```rust
if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
    // Standout did not handle this command; fall back to legacy dispatch.
    legacy_dispatch();
}
```

Parses args, dispatches to a handler, and performs the final write. It returns
`true` when Standout handled the command and `false` for an unmatched fallback.
Help/version and successes use stdout/status 0, usage errors use stderr/status
2, and runtime/write failures use stderr/status 1. The two owner-declared
failures are the exceptions: `AppFailure` carries the application's own nonzero
status and verbatim stderr payload, and `ExternalFailure` preserves an
authoritative external operation's. See [Error Handling](./error-handling.md).

### Capture Output

For tests, reach for `standout_test::TestHarness` (see [Testing](./testing.md)).
For post-processing, or any other embedding caller that needs the output
string, pass destination properties and input sources in explicitly:

```rust
let target = TargetProperties::detect();
let sources = InputSources::from_process();
let result = app.run_with(cmd, args, target, sources);
let _ = result.warnings();
match result.into_outcome() {
    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => { /* use output string */ }
    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => { /* handle binary */ }
    DispatchResult::Error(error) => { /* inspect error.kind() */ }
    DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches) => { /* fallback dispatch */ }
    _ => {}
}
```

Returns `CompletedRun` instead of printing: a wrapper around `DispatchResult`
plus framework warnings. Use `exit_status()`, `success_kind()`, and
`error_kind()` for typed assertions; see [Execution
Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md).

### Parse Only

```rust
match app.get_matches_from(cmd, std::env::args(), &InputSources::from_process()) {
    HelpResult::Matches(matches) => { /* use matches for manual dispatch */ }
    HelpResult::Help(text) | HelpResult::PagedHelp(text) => { /* the invocation asked for help */ }
    HelpResult::Error(e) => { /* a clap::Error: usage failure, or --version display */ }
}
```

Parses with Standout's augmented command, intercepting help display; returns
matches only when the invocation didn't trigger a help/usage/version display.

## Build Validation

`build()` validates:

- a theme registry exists and contains the theme named by `.default_theme(...)`
- named templates resolve through `.templates(...)` or `.templates_dir(...)`
- convention templates resolve when application templates are configured; without application templates, human-mode rendering reports the missing convention template at runtime
- registered templates compile
- framework templates only use tags defined by the resolved theme
- `command_groups`, topics, and `help_word(true)` are not combined with `.help_handling(false)`
- commands do not collide with the `help` word standout installs when help handling is on
- the same command path and hook phase are not configured through both `CommandConfig` and `AppBuilder::hooks`

What's NOT validated at build time:

- Command handlers
- Hook signatures (verified at registration)

## Complete Example

```rust
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, FnHandler, HandlerResult, Output};
use standout_macros::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
use clap::{Command, ArgMatches};
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListOutput {
    items: Vec<String>,
}

fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
    let items = vec!["one".into(), "two".into()];
    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items }))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let cli = Command::new("myapp")
        .subcommand(Command::new("list").about("List items"));

    let app = App::builder()
        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
        .default_theme("default")
        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
        .context("version", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION").into())
        .command_with("list", FnHandler::new(list_handler), |config| {
            config.template_name("list")
        })?
        .topics_dir("docs/topics")?
        .build()?;

    app.run(cli, std::env::args());
    Ok(())
}
```

Template `src/templates/list.j2`:

```jinja

{% for item in items %}
  - {{ item }}
{% endfor %}

[muted]v{{ version }}[/muted]
```

Style `src/styles/default.css`:

```css
.header { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
.muted { opacity: 0.5; }
```

# Passthrough Commands

Every other way of registering a command — the `Dispatch` derive,
`command_with`, a `#[handler]` function — assumes the handler hands back
something serializable that Standout can render or serialize. A passthrough
command is the one registration shape without that assumption: the handler
writes its own bytes and returns `Result<(), anyhow::Error>`. ADR-0032 keeps
it as a secondary path for that reason: nothing else on the registration axis
accepts a signature with no serializable output and no render.

Reach for it when a command's job is genuinely "run this external process and
let it own the terminal" — streaming a subprocess's output live, driving an
interactive prompt library that writes ANSI itself, or wrapping a tool that
already produces its own formatted output — not for handlers that happen to
print instead of returning data.

## API

```rust
impl AppBuilder {
    pub fn command_passthrough<F>(self, path: &str, handler: F) -> Result<Self, SetupError>
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

For a command declared inside `.commands(|g| ...)`, `GroupBuilder` has the
matching entry point:

```rust
impl GroupBuilder {
    pub fn passthrough<F>(self, name: &str, handler: F) -> Self
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

Both take the same closure shape and register the command with no template:
there is nothing for a template to render.

## What it does not get

A passthrough command has no `Output` enum to return, so it gets none of the
things that come from having one:

- No template. The command is registered with its template reference set to
  "absent, silently" — there is no configured or conventional template to
  resolve, by design, not by omission.
- No render pass, so no theme, no style tags, no `Tabular` columns.
- No structured output modes. `Output::Render` is what `--output json` (and
  `yaml`/`xml`/`csv`) serializes; a passthrough handler never produces an
  `Output` value, so those modes have nothing to act on.
- No post-dispatch hooks. The passthrough dispatch closure is handed the
  command's `Hooks` and ignores them, so nothing runs between the handler
  returning and the empty result leaving dispatch.

App-level hooks registered for the command's path *do* still run, because they
sit outside the dispatch closure: a pre-dispatch hook runs before the handler
as it would for any command, and a post-output hook runs after it, receiving
`RenderedOutput::Silent`. A post-output hook attached to a passthrough command
is therefore not inert — it observes and can act, it just has no rendered text
to transform.

Concretely, under `--output json` (or any other output mode) a passthrough
command runs exactly the same as under the default: the dispatch closure
backing `command_passthrough`/`passthrough` takes the output mode as a
parameter and ignores it. Standout's own output-writing pipeline resolves the
command to an empty string every time — whatever the handler wrote, it wrote
directly (to stdout, stderr, a file, wherever), outside that pipeline, and
`--output` has no way to reach it.

## What the handler is responsible for

Because nothing downstream will format or emit anything on the handler's
behalf, the handler owns:

- Writing everything it wants seen — to stdout, stderr, or elsewhere.
- Its own error reporting for anything it prints before returning `Err(...)`;
  the `anyhow::Error` becomes the command's failure, but text already written
  stays written.
- Respecting (or explicitly ignoring) the user's terminal — colors, width,
  paging — since none of the framework's rendering machinery runs.

## Worked example

```rust
use anyhow::Context;
use clap::ArgMatches;
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext};
use std::process::Command;

fn run_migrations(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    let status = Command::new("./migrate.sh")
        .status()
        .context("failed to launch migrate.sh")?;
    if !status.success() {
        anyhow::bail!("migrate.sh exited with {status}");
    }
    Ok(())
}

let app = App::builder()
    .command_passthrough("migrate", run_migrations)?
    .build()?;
```

`migrate.sh`'s own stdout and stderr reach the terminal unchanged; Standout
neither captures nor reformats them.

## When not to use it

The blessed path is a `#[handler]` function returning `Result<T, E>`, wrapped
in `Output::Render` and rendered through a template — see
[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md). Reach for
that whenever the command has any data a caller might want as JSON, any
output a template could format, or any reason to support `--output`. Use
passthrough only when the handler's whole job is to hand control to
something else that already owns its own bytes.

1	# Seeker: Filtering, Ordering, and Query Strings
2	
3	Commands that list something almost always grow filter flags: `--status`,
4	`--name-contains`, `--priority-gte`, `--order-by`. Seeker is the crate behind
5	`standout::seeker` that gives those filters a single implementation: a
6	`Query` built either programmatically or by parsing a flat set of key/value
7	pairs (typically `--filter key=value` flags, or a raw query string), run
8	against a slice of items through a per-type accessor function.
9	
10	Reach for it when a command needs to filter, sort, or paginate an in-memory
11	collection and you want the filter vocabulary (`eq`, `contains`, `gte`,
12	`before`, `in`, ordering, `limit`/`offset`) to be consistent across commands
13	instead of each one inventing its own flags.
14	
15	## Where it lives
16	
17	```rust
18	use standout::seeker::{
19	    Dir, Op, OrderBy, Query, SeekType, SeekerEnum, SeekerSchema, Seekable, Value, parse_query,
20	};
21	use standout::Seekable; // #[derive(Seekable)]
22	```
23	
24	`standout::seeker` is a re-export of the `standout-seeker` crate
25	(`pub use standout_seeker as seeker;`); the derive macro is
26	`standout_macros::Seekable`, re-exported as `standout::Seekable`.
27	
28	## Deriving `Seekable`
29	
30	`#[derive(Seekable)]` on a struct with named fields generates:
31	
32	- An implementation of the `Seekable` trait: `seeker_field_value(&self, field:
33	  &str) -> Value<'_>`, the trait's one required method. The
34	  `Self::accessor(item, field)` function `Query::filter` and friends expect is
35	  a provided method on the trait, so it comes with any implementation, derived
36	  or written by hand.
37	- An implementation of `SeekerSchema`, providing `field_type(field)` and
38	  `field_names()` — this is what `parse_query` uses to validate a query string
39	  against the struct's actual fields. It does **not** provide
40	  `resolve_enum_variant(field, variant)`, which keeps the trait's default
41	  `None`; see [Enum fields](#enum-fields) for what that costs.
42	- One `pub const` per seekable field, upper-cased (`NAME`, `CREATED_AT`), so
43	  callers write `Task::PRIORITY` instead of the string literal `"priority"`.
44	
45	Each field opts in with a `#[seek(...)]` attribute; unannotated fields are
46	skipped entirely (not queryable, no constant, absent from `field_names()`).
47	
48	| `#[seek(...)]` key | Effect |
49	| --- | --- |
50	| `String` / `string` | Field type is `SeekType::String` |
51	| `Number` / `number` | Field type is `SeekType::Number` |
52	| `Timestamp` / `timestamp` | Field type is `SeekType::Timestamp` (the field type must implement `SeekerTimestamp`; `i64` and `u64` do out of the box, read as milliseconds) |
53	| `Enum` / `enumeration` | Field type is `SeekType::Enum` (the field type must implement `SeekerEnum`) |
54	| `Bool` / `boolean` / `bool` | Field type is `SeekType::Bool` |
55	| `ty = "string"` (etc.) | Same five types, spelled as a string literal instead of a bare identifier |
56	| `skip` | Field is not queryable and gets no constant |
57	| `rename = "name"` | The query-facing field name differs from the Rust field name |
58	
59	`String`/`Number`/etc. and `rename`/`ty` combine on the same attribute:
60	`#[seek(String, rename = "title")]`. A field with no `#[seek(...)]` attribute
61	at all is treated the same as `#[seek(skip)]`.
62	
63	## Building a `Query` by hand
64	
65	```rust
66	let query = Query::new()
67	    .and_gte(Task::PRIORITY, 4i32)
68	    .not_eq(Task::DONE, true)
69	    .order_desc(Task::PRIORITY)
70	    .limit(20)
71	    .build();
72	
73	let results = query.filter(&tasks, Task::accessor);
74	```
75	
76	`Query` holds three clause groups — `and`, `or`, `not` — combined with fixed
77	semantics: an item matches when *all* `and` clauses match, *and* (any `or`
78	clause matches, or there are none), *and* no `not` clause matches. Each group
79	builds with `.and(field, op, value)` / `.or(...)` / `.not(...)`, or a
80	per-operator shortcut (`.and_eq`, `.and_gt`, `.and_contains`,
81	`.and_before`, `.and_in`, and their `or_`/`not_` counterparts). `.order_by`,
82	`.order_asc`, `.order_desc`, `.limit`, and `.offset` configure the rest.
83	`.filter` returns matching references in order; `.filter_cloned`,
84	`.filter_mut`, `.count`, `.any`, `.all`, `.find`, and `.position` cover the
85	other common shapes.
86	
87	## The query string grammar
88	
89	`parse_query::<S>(pairs)` turns an ordered sequence of `(key, value)` string
90	pairs into a `Query`, validating every *clause* field and operator against `S:
91	SeekerSchema`. This is the shape a `--filter` flag or a raw query string
92	typically produces.
93	
94	**Field clauses** — a key is either a bare field name (using the field's
95	default operator: `Eq` for everything except `Bool`, which defaults to `Is`)
96	or `field-operator`:
97	
98	```text
99	name=docs                  # name eq "docs"
100	name-contains=docs         # name contains "docs"
101	priority-gte=4             # priority >= 4
102	created-at-before=2024-01-01
103	status-in=1,2              # enum field, comma-separated discriminants
104	                           # (variant names too, on a hand-written schema)
105	done                       # bare boolean flag => done eq true
106	```
107	
108	Recognized operators (case-insensitive) and their aliases:
109	`eq`, `ne`/`neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `startswith`/`prefix`,
110	`endswith`/`suffix`, `contains`, `regex`/`re`/`match`, `before`, `after`,
111	`in`, `is`. A compound field name like `created-at` still parses correctly
112	when combined with an operator (`created-at-before`), because only the last
113	hyphen-separated segment is checked against the operator list.
114	
115	**Group markers** — the bare keys `AND`, `OR`, and `NOT` (case-insensitive)
116	switch which clause group subsequent pairs join, starting from `AND`:
117	
118	```text
119	name-contains=a&OR&name-contains=b&NOT&done=true
120	```
121	
122	**Ordering, limit, offset** — reserved keys, not field clauses:
123	
124	```text
125	order=priority-desc   # also: orderby, order-by, sort
126	limit=10
127	offset=5              # also: skip
128	```
129	
130	`order`'s value is `field` (ascending) or `field-asc`/`field-desc`. The
131	ordering field is **not** checked against the schema: `parse_query` reads the
132	reserved `order`/`sort` key before it consults `S::field_type`, so
133	`order=does-not-exist` parses without error and then sorts every item on
134	`Value::None`, leaving the input order. Validate an ordering field yourself
135	against `S::field_names()` if a typo there should be an error.
136	
137	**Value parsing per field type:**
138	
139	- String: taken verbatim, unless the operator is `regex` (compiled as a
140	  regular expression).
141	- Number: tried as `i64`, then `u64`, then `f64`.
142	- Timestamp: a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, `YYYY-MM-DD`, an ISO
143	  datetime (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fff]Z`), or a bare four-digit year.
144	- Enum: a numeric discriminant, or a variant name resolved through
145	  `SeekerSchema::resolve_enum_variant`; `in` accepts a comma-separated list
146	  of either. See [Enum fields](#enum-fields) — a derived schema takes
147	  discriminants only.
148	- Bool: `true`/`1`/`yes`/`on` or `false`/`0`/`no`/`off` (case-insensitive);
149	  an empty value defaults to `true`.
150	
151	An unknown *clause* field, an operator invalid for the field's type
152	(`name-gt`, since strings don't support `Gt`), or an unparsable value each
153	produce a `ParseError` naming the field and, for unknown fields, the schema's
154	actual `field_names()`. The reserved `order`/`sort` key is the exception noted
155	above.
156	
157	## Enum fields
158	
159	`SeekerSchema::resolve_enum_variant(field, variant)` is what turns
160	`status=pending` into a discriminant, and it defaults to returning `None`.
161	`#[derive(Seekable)]` does not override it, so a **derived schema matches enum
162	fields on numeric discriminants only** — `status=pending` fails with a parse
163	error, `status=0` works. Because the derive owns the whole `SeekerSchema`
164	implementation, a second `impl` cannot add the method beside it.
165	
166	To match on variant names, drop the derive for that struct and write both
167	traits by hand — `Seekable` for the values, `SeekerSchema` for the schema plus
168	the variant mapping. You give up the generated field constants along with it — `accessor` still
169	comes from the trait:
170	
171	```rust
172	#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
173	enum Status {
174	    Pending = 0,
175	    Active = 1,
176	}
177	
178	impl SeekerEnum for Status {
179	    fn seeker_discriminant(&self) -> u32 {
180	        *self as u32
181	    }
182	}
183	
184	struct Task {
185	    name: String,
186	    status: Status,
187	}
188	
189	impl Seekable for Task {
190	    fn seeker_field_value(&self, field: &str) -> Value<'_> {
191	        match field {
192	            "name" => Value::String(&self.name),
193	            "status" => Value::Enum(self.status.seeker_discriminant()),
194	            _ => Value::None,
195	        }
196	    }
197	}
198	
199	impl SeekerSchema for Task {
200	    fn field_type(field: &str) -> Option<SeekType> {
201	        match field {
202	            "name" => Some(SeekType::String),
203	            "status" => Some(SeekType::Enum),
204	            _ => None,
205	        }
206	    }
207	
208	    fn field_names() -> &'static [&'static str] {
209	        &["name", "status"]
210	    }
211	
212	    fn resolve_enum_variant(field: &str, variant: &str) -> Option<u32> {
213	        match (field, variant) {
214	            ("status", "pending") => Some(Status::Pending as u32),
215	            ("status", "active") => Some(Status::Active as u32),
216	            _ => None,
217	        }
218	    }
219	}
220	```
221	
222	`parse_query::<Task>` now accepts `status=pending` and `status-in=pending,active`
223	as well as the discriminants.
224	
225	## Example
226	
227	```rust
228	#[derive(Seekable)]
229	struct Task {
230	    #[seek(String)]
231	    name: String,
232	    #[seek(Number)]
233	    priority: i32,
234	    #[seek(Bool)]
235	    done: bool,
236	}
237	
238	let pairs = vec![
239	    ("priority-gte".to_string(), "4".to_string()),
240	    ("NOT".to_string(), "".to_string()),
241	    ("done".to_string(), "true".to_string()),
242	];
243	let query = parse_query::<Task>(pairs)?;
244	let results = query.filter(&tasks, Task::accessor);
245	```
246

clause matches, or there are none), *and* no `not` clause matches. Each group
builds with `.and(field, op, value)` / `.or(...)` / `.not(...)`, or a
per-operator shortcut (`.and_eq`, `.and_gt`, `.and_contains`,
`.and_before`, `.and_in`, and their `or_`/`not_` counterparts). `.order_by`,
`.order_asc`, `.order_desc`, `.limit`, and `.offset` configure the rest.
`.filter` returns matching references in order; `.filter_cloned`,
`.filter_mut`, `.count`, `.any`, `.all`, `.find`, and `.position` cover the
other common shapes.

## The query string grammar

`parse_query::<S>(pairs)` turns an ordered sequence of `(key, value)` string
pairs into a `Query`, validating every *clause* field and operator against `S:
SeekerSchema`. This is the shape a `--filter` flag or a raw query string
typically produces.

**Field clauses** — a key is either a bare field name (using the field's
default operator: `Eq` for everything except `Bool`, which defaults to `Is`)
or `field-operator`:

```text
name=docs                  # name eq "docs"
name-contains=docs         # name contains "docs"
priority-gte=4             # priority >= 4
created-at-before=2024-01-01
status-in=1,2              # enum field, comma-separated discriminants
                           # (variant names too, on a hand-written schema)
done                       # bare boolean flag => done eq true
```

Recognized operators (case-insensitive) and their aliases:
`eq`, `ne`/`neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `startswith`/`prefix`,
`endswith`/`suffix`, `contains`, `regex`/`re`/`match`, `before`, `after`,
`in`, `is`. A compound field name like `created-at` still parses correctly
when combined with an operator (`created-at-before`), because only the last
hyphen-separated segment is checked against the operator list.

**Group markers** — the bare keys `AND`, `OR`, and `NOT` (case-insensitive)
switch which clause group subsequent pairs join, starting from `AND`:

```text
name-contains=a&OR&name-contains=b&NOT&done=true
```

**Ordering, limit, offset** — reserved keys, not field clauses:

```text
order=priority-desc   # also: orderby, order-by, sort
limit=10
offset=5              # also: skip
```

`order`'s value is `field` (ascending) or `field-asc`/`field-desc`. The
ordering field is **not** checked against the schema: `parse_query` reads the
reserved `order`/`sort` key before it consults `S::field_type`, so
`order=does-not-exist` parses without error and then sorts every item on
`Value::None`, leaving the input order. Validate an ordering field yourself
against `S::field_names()` if a typo there should be an error.

**Value parsing per field type:**

- String: taken verbatim, unless the operator is `regex` (compiled as a
  regular expression).
- Number: tried as `i64`, then `u64`, then `f64`.
- Timestamp: a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, `YYYY-MM-DD`, an ISO
  datetime (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fff]Z`), or a bare four-digit year.
- Enum: a numeric discriminant, or a variant name resolved through
  `SeekerSchema::resolve_enum_variant`; `in` accepts a comma-separated list
  of either. See [Enum fields](#enum-fields) — a derived schema takes
  discriminants only.
- Bool: `true`/`1`/`yes`/`on` or `false`/`0`/`no`/`off` (case-insensitive);
  an empty value defaults to `true`.

An unknown *clause* field, an operator invalid for the field's type
(`name-gt`, since strings don't support `Gt`), or an unparsable value each
produce a `ParseError` naming the field and, for unknown fields, the schema's
actual `field_names()`. The reserved `order`/`sort` key is the exception noted
above.

## Enum fields

`SeekerSchema::resolve_enum_variant(field, variant)` is what turns
`status=pending` into a discriminant, and it defaults to returning `None`.
`#[derive(Seekable)]` does not override it, so a **derived schema matches enum
fields on numeric discriminants only** — `status=pending` fails with a parse
error, `status=0` works. Because the derive owns the whole `SeekerSchema`
implementation, a second `impl` cannot add the method beside it.

To match on variant names, drop the derive for that struct and write both
traits by hand — `Seekable` for the values, `SeekerSchema` for the schema plus
the variant mapping. You give up the generated field constants along with it — `accessor` still
comes from the trait:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum Status {
    Pending = 0,
    Active = 1,
}

impl SeekerEnum for Status {
    fn seeker_discriminant(&self) -> u32 {
        *self as u32
    }
}

struct Task {
    name: String,
    status: Status,
}

impl Seekable for Task {
    fn seeker_field_value(&self, field: &str) -> Value<'_> {
        match field {
            "name" => Value::String(&self.name),
            "status" => Value::Enum(self.status.seeker_discriminant()),
            _ => Value::None,
        }
    }
}

impl SeekerSchema for Task {
    fn field_type(field: &str) -> Option<SeekType> {
        match field {
            "name" => Some(SeekType::String),
            "status" => Some(SeekType::Enum),
            _ => None,
        }
    }

    fn field_names() -> &'static [&'static str] {
        &["name", "status"]
    }

    fn resolve_enum_variant(field: &str, variant: &str) -> Option<u32> {
        match (field, variant) {
            ("status", "pending") => Some(Status::Pending as u32),
            ("status", "active") => Some(Status::Active as u32),
            _ => None,
        }
    }
}
```

`parse_query::<Task>` now accepts `status=pending` and `status-in=pending,active`
as well as the discriminants.

## Example

```rust
#[derive(Seekable)]
struct Task {
    #[seek(String)]
    name: String,
    #[seek(Number)]
    priority: i32,
    #[seek(Bool)]
    done: bool,
}

let pairs = vec![
    ("priority-gte".to_string(), "4".to_string()),
    ("NOT".to_string(), "".to_string()),
    ("done".to_string(), "true".to_string()),
];
let query = parse_query::<Task>(pairs)?;
let results = query.filter(&tasks, Task::accessor);
```

1	# Output Modes
2	
3	Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.
4	
5	The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.
6	
7	## The OutputMode Enum
8	
9	```rust
10	pub enum OutputMode {
11	    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
12	    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
13	    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
14	    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
15	    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
16	    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
17	    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
18	    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
19	}
20	```
21	
22	Three categories:
23	
24	**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.
25	
26	**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.
27	
28	**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.
29	
30	## Auto Mode
31	
32	`Auto` is the default when `--output` is absent, and an application can change
33	that default with
34	[`output_mode_fallback(mode)`](./app-configuration.md#output-mode-fallback) — an
35	explicit `--output` still outranks it. `Auto` queries the terminal for color
36	support:
37	
38	```rust
39	Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
40	```
41	
42	If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).
43	
44	This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:
45	
46	```bash
47	myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
48	myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
49	myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
50	```
51	
52	## The --output Flag
53	
54	Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:
55	
56	```bash
57	myapp list --output=auto        # Default
58	myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
59	myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
60	myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
61	myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
62	myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
63	myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
64	myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
65	```
66	
67	The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.
68	
69	## Term vs Text
70	
71	**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
72	when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:
73	
74	```bash
75	myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
76	```
77	
78	Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).
79	
80	A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
81	not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
82	same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
83	is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
84	the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
85	that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
86	`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
87	`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
88	into `term`.
89	
90	**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:
91	
92	```bash
93	myapp list --output=text
94	```
95	
96	Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.
97	
98	Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
99	writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
100	those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
101	them itself.
102	
103	`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
104	them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
105	release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
106	against `term` or `text`.
107	
108	## TermDebug Mode
109	
110	TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:
111	
112	```text
113	Template: [title]Hello[/title]
114	Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
115	```
116	
117	Use cases:
118	
119	- Debugging template issues
120	- Verifying style tag placement
121	- Automated testing of template output
122	
123	Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
124	TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
125	style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.
126	
127	## Structured Modes
128	
129	Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:
130	
131	```rust
132	#[derive(Serialize)]
133	struct ListOutput {
134	    items: Vec<Item>,
135	    total: usize,
136	}
137	
138	fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
139	    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
140	}
141	```
142	
143	```bash
144	myapp list --output=json
145	```
146	
147	```json
148	{
149	  "items": [...],
150	  "total": 42
151	}
152	```
153	
154	Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:
155	
156	- Machine-readable output for scripts
157	- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
158	- API-like behavior from CLI apps
159	
160	### CSV Output
161	
162	Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
163	CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
164	should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.
165	
166	The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
167	a caller needs explicit columns and headers:
168	
169	```rust
170	use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
171	use standout::OutputMode;
172	use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;
173	
174	let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
175	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
176	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
177	    .build();
178	
179	render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
180	```
181	
182	The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).
183	
184	When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
185	attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:
186	
187	```rust
188	use serde_json::json;
189	use standout::cli::FnHandler;
190	use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
191	use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};
192	
193	let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
194	    CsvProjection::builder("items")
195	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
196	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
197	        .derived_column(
198	            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
199	            |row, _root| json!(
200	                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
201	                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
202	            ),
203	        )
204	        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
205	            "language": "TOTAL",
206	            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
207	            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
208	        }))
209	        .conditional_row(|root| {
210	            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
211	                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
212	        })
213	        .build(),
214	);
215	
216	App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
217	    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
218	})?;
219	```
220	
221	Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
222	columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
223	callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
224	ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.
225	
226	The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
227	template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
228	pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
229	after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
230	therefore all observe the same projected CSV.
231	
232	See [Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for
233	tabular specifications and layout.
234	
235	## File Output
236	
237	The `--output-file-path` flag redirects output to a file:
238	
239	```bash
240	myapp list --output-file-path=results.txt
241	myapp list --output=json --output-file-path=data.json
242	```
243	
244	Behavior:
245	
246	- Text output: written to file, nothing printed to stdout
247	- Binary output: written to the requested file instead of stdout
248	- Silent output: no-op
249	
250	After writing to file, stdout output is suppressed to prevent double-printing.
251	
252	## Customizing Flags
253	
254	Rename or disable the flags via `AppBuilder`:
255	
256	```rust
257	App::builder()
258	    .output_flag(Some("format"))       // --format instead of --output
259	    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))     // --out instead of --output-file-path
260	    .build()?
261	```
262	
263	```rust
264	App::builder()
265	    .no_output_flag()                  // Disable --output entirely
266	    .no_output_file_flag()             // Disable file output
267	    .build()?
268	```
269	
270	## Keep Output Mode Out of Handlers
271	
272	Output mode is a rendering concern and is deliberately absent from
273	`CommandContext`. A handler should return the same serializable data regardless
274	of whether the caller selected terminal, text, or structured output. If a
275	command's behavior genuinely differs, model that as an explicit command or
276	argument rather than an implicit presentation-mode branch.
277	
278	## Rendering Without CLI
279	
280	For standalone rendering with explicit mode:
281	
282	```rust
283	use standout::{render_auto, OutputMode};
284	
285	// Renders template for Term/Text, serializes for Json/Yaml
286	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
287	```
288	
289	The "auto" in `render_auto` refers to template-vs-serialize dispatch, not color detection.
290	
291	For full control over both output mode and color mode:
292	
293	```rust
294	use standout::{render_with_mode, ColorMode};
295	
296	let output = render_with_mode(
297	    template,
298	    &data,
299	    &theme,
300	    OutputMode::Term,
301	    ColorMode::Dark,
302	)?;
303	```
304
