1	# The Topics System
2	
3	Standout provides a dedicated help topics system because command help (`--help`) is a poor place for conceptual documentation.
4	
5	Arguments and flags describe *mechanics*, but complex applications need longer-form guides for *concepts*—configuration formats, authentication flows, or troubleshooting. The Topics system integrates these directly into your CLI, accessible via `myapp help <topic>`, keeping users in the terminal.
6	
7	## What Topics Are For
8	
9	Command help describes flags and arguments. Topics explain broader concepts:
10	
11	- Configuration file format
12	- Authentication setup
13	- Workflow guides
14	- Troubleshooting
15	
16	```bash
17	myapp help                  # Shows commands + available topics
18	myapp help auth             # Shows the "auth" topic
19	myapp help config-format    # Shows the "config-format" topic
20	myapp help auth --page      # Shows topic in a pager
21	```
22	
23	## The Topic Struct
24	
25	```rust
26	pub struct Topic {
27	    pub title: String,        // Display title: "Authentication Setup"
28	    pub content: String,      // Full content
29	    pub topic_type: TopicType, // Text or Markdown
30	    pub name: String,         // URL-safe slug: "authentication-setup"
31	}
32	
33	pub enum TopicType {
34	    Text,
35	    Markdown,
36	    Unknown,
37	}
38	```
39	
40	The `name` is a URL-safe slug used in `help <name>`. If not provided, it's auto-generated from the title:
41	
42	- "Hello World" → `hello-world`
43	- "Café Setup" → `cafe-setup`
44	
45	## Adding Topics
46	
47	### Programmatically
48	
49	```rust
50	use standout::topics::{Topic, TopicType};
51	
52	let topic = Topic::new(
53	    "Configuration Format",
54	    "The config file uses YAML format...",
55	    TopicType::Text,
56	    None,  // Auto-generate name from title
57	);
58	
59	App::builder()
60	    .add_topic(topic)
61	    .build()?
62	```
63	
64	### From a Directory
65	
66	```rust
67	App::builder()
68	    .topics_dir("docs/topics")
69	    .build()?
70	```
71	
72	Standout scans the directory for `.txt` and `.md` files. File format:
73	
74	```text
75	Configuration Format
76	
77	The config file uses YAML format.
78	Place it in ~/.myapp/config.yaml.
79	
80	Supported keys:
81	- theme: color theme name
82	- output: default output mode
83	```
84	
85	First non-blank line becomes the title. Everything after becomes content. The filename (without extension) becomes the topic name.
86	
87	Directory structure:
88	
89	```text
90	docs/topics/
91	  config-format.txt      # Topic name: config-format
92	  authentication.md      # Topic name: authentication
93	  getting-started.txt    # Topic name: getting-started
94	```
95	
96	## TopicRegistry
97	
98	`TopicRegistry` stores and retrieves topics:
99	
100	```rust
101	let mut registry = TopicRegistry::new();
102	registry.add_topic(topic1);
103	registry.add_topic(topic2);
104	
105	// Retrieve
106	if let Some(topic) = registry.get_topic("config-format") {
107	    println!("{}", topic.content);
108	}
109	
110	// List all (sorted by name)
111	for topic in registry.list_topics() {
112	    println!("{}: {}", topic.name, topic.title);
113	}
114	```
115	
116	Duplicate topic names cause a panic—each name must be unique.
117	
118	## Help Integration
119	
120	Topics automatically appear in help output:
121	
122	```text
123	myapp help
124	
125	USAGE
126	  myapp <COMMAND>
127	
128	COMMANDS
129	  list       List items
130	  add        Add an item
131	  config     Manage configuration
132	
133	LEARN MORE
134	  auth               Authentication Setup
135	  config-format      Configuration Format
136	  getting-started    Getting Started
137	```
138	
139	The "LEARN MORE" section lists all registered topics. Users run `myapp help <topic-name>` to view the full content.
140	
141	## Pager Support
142	
143	For long topics, the `--page` flag displays content through a pager:
144	
145	```bash
146	myapp help getting-started --page
147	```
148	
149	Standout tries pagers in order:
150	
151	1. `$PAGER` environment variable
152	2. `less`
153	3. `more`
154	4. Falls back to printing directly if none available
155	
156	## Rendering Topics
157	
158	For custom topic rendering outside the help system:
159	
160	```rust
161	use standout::topics::{render_topic, render_topics_list, TopicRenderConfig};
162	
163	// Render single topic
164	let output = render_topic(&topic, None)?;
165	
166	// Render list of all topics
167	let list = render_topics_list(&registry, "myapp help <topic>", None)?;
168	
169	// With custom config
170	let config = TopicRenderConfig {
171	    theme: Some(my_theme),
172	    output_mode: Some(OutputMode::Text),
173	    ..Default::default()
174	};
175	let output = render_topic(&topic, Some(config))?;
176	```
177	
178	## Topic Templates
179	
180	Topics are rendered through templates with style tags:
181	
182	**Single topic template:**
183	
184	```jinja
185	[header]{{ title | upper }}[/header]
186	
187	{{ content }}
188	```
189	
190	**Topic list template:**
191	
192	```jinja
193	[about]Available Topics[/about]
194	
195	[header]USAGE[/header]
196	  [usage]{{ usage }}[/usage]
197	
198	[header]TOPICS[/header]
199	{%- for topic in topics %}
200	  {{ ("[item]" ~ topic.name ~ "[/item]") | pad_right(name_width) }}  [desc]{{ topic.title }}[/desc]
201	{%- endfor %}
202	```
203	
204	Override via `TopicRenderConfig`:
205	
206	```rust
207	let config = TopicRenderConfig {
208	    topic_template: Some(my_template.into()),
209	    list_template: Some(my_list_template.into()),
210	    ..Default::default()
211	};
212	```
213	
214	## Markdown Topics
215	
216	Topics with `.md` extension or `TopicType::Markdown` can contain Markdown formatting. Standout renders Markdown appropriately for the terminal when displaying.
217	
218	```markdown
219	# Getting Started
220	
221	Install the application:
222	
223	    cargo install myapp
224	
225	Then create a configuration file...
226	```
227	
228	The topic type is inferred from file extension when loading from directories.
229

- Configuration file format
- Authentication setup
- Workflow guides
- Troubleshooting

```bash
myapp help                  # Shows commands + available topics
myapp help auth             # Shows the "auth" topic
myapp help config-format    # Shows the "config-format" topic
myapp help auth --page      # Shows topic in a pager
```

## The Topic Struct

```rust
pub struct Topic {
    pub title: String,        // Display title: "Authentication Setup"
    pub content: String,      // Full content
    pub topic_type: TopicType, // Text or Markdown
    pub name: String,         // URL-safe slug: "authentication-setup"
}

pub enum TopicType {
    Text,
    Markdown,
    Unknown,
}
```

The `name` is a URL-safe slug used in `help <name>`. If not provided, it's auto-generated from the title:

- "Hello World" → `hello-world`
- "Café Setup" → `cafe-setup`

## Adding Topics

### Programmatically

```rust
use standout::topics::{Topic, TopicType};

let topic = Topic::new(
    "Configuration Format",
    "The config file uses YAML format...",
    TopicType::Text,
    None,  // Auto-generate name from title
);

App::builder()
    .add_topic(topic)
    .build()?
```

### From a Directory

```rust
App::builder()
    .topics_dir("docs/topics")
    .build()?
```

Standout scans the directory for `.txt` and `.md` files. File format:

```text
Configuration Format

The config file uses YAML format.
Place it in ~/.myapp/config.yaml.

Supported keys:
- theme: color theme name
- output: default output mode
```

First non-blank line becomes the title. Everything after becomes content. The filename (without extension) becomes the topic name.

Directory structure:

```text
docs/topics/
  config-format.txt      # Topic name: config-format
  authentication.md      # Topic name: authentication
  getting-started.txt    # Topic name: getting-started
```

## TopicRegistry

`TopicRegistry` stores and retrieves topics:

```rust
let mut registry = TopicRegistry::new();
registry.add_topic(topic1);
registry.add_topic(topic2);

// Retrieve
if let Some(topic) = registry.get_topic("config-format") {
    println!("{}", topic.content);
}

// List all (sorted by name)
for topic in registry.list_topics() {
    println!("{}: {}", topic.name, topic.title);
}
```

Duplicate topic names cause a panic—each name must be unique.

## Help Integration

Topics automatically appear in help output:

```text
myapp help

USAGE
  myapp <COMMAND>

COMMANDS
  list       List items
  add        Add an item
  config     Manage configuration

LEARN MORE
  auth               Authentication Setup
  config-format      Configuration Format
  getting-started    Getting Started
```

The "LEARN MORE" section lists all registered topics. Users run `myapp help <topic-name>` to view the full content.

## Pager Support

For long topics, the `--page` flag displays content through a pager:

```bash
myapp help getting-started --page
```

Standout tries pagers in order:

1. `$PAGER` environment variable
2. `less`
3. `more`
4. Falls back to printing directly if none available

## Rendering Topics

For custom topic rendering outside the help system:

```rust
use standout::topics::{render_topic, render_topics_list, TopicRenderConfig};

// Render single topic
let output = render_topic(&topic, None)?;

// Render list of all topics
let list = render_topics_list(&registry, "myapp help <topic>", None)?;

// With custom config
let config = TopicRenderConfig {
    theme: Some(my_theme),
    output_mode: Some(OutputMode::Text),
    ..Default::default()
};
let output = render_topic(&topic, Some(config))?;
```

## Topic Templates

Topics are rendered through templates with style tags:

**Single topic template:**

```jinja
[header]{{ title | upper }}[/header]

{{ content }}
```

**Topic list template:**

```jinja
[about]Available Topics[/about]

[header]USAGE[/header]
  [usage]{{ usage }}[/usage]

[header]TOPICS[/header]
{%- for topic in topics %}
  {{ ("[item]" ~ topic.name ~ "[/item]") | pad_right(name_width) }}  [desc]{{ topic.title }}[/desc]
{%- endfor %}
```

Override via `TopicRenderConfig`:

```rust
let config = TopicRenderConfig {
    topic_template: Some(my_template.into()),
    list_template: Some(my_list_template.into()),
    ..Default::default()
};
```

## Markdown Topics

Topics with `.md` extension or `TopicType::Markdown` can contain Markdown formatting. Standout renders Markdown appropriately for the terminal when displaying.

```markdown
# Getting Started

Install the application:

    cargo install myapp

Then create a configuration file...
```

The topic type is inferred from file extension when loading from directories.

1	# Templating
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a two-pass templating system that combines a template engine for logic and data binding with a custom BBCode-like syntax for styling. This separation keeps templates readable while providing full control over both content and presentation.
4	
5	The default engine is MiniJinja (Jinja2-compatible), but alternative engines are available. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for options including a lightweight `SimpleEngine` for reduced binary size.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Two-Pass Rendering Pipeline
10	
11	Templates are processed in two distinct passes:
12	
13	```text
14	Template + Data → [Pass 1: MiniJinja] → Text with style tags → [Pass 2: BBParser] → Final output
15	```
16	
17	**Pass 1 - MiniJinja**: Standard template processing. Variables are substituted, control flow executes, filters apply.
18	
19	**Pass 2 - BBParser**: Style tag processing. Bracket-notation tags are converted to ANSI escape codes (or stripped, depending on output mode).
20	
21	### Pipeline Example
22	
23	```text
24	Template:     [title]{{ name }}[/title] has {{ count }} items
25	Data:         { name: "Report", count: 42 }
26	
27	After Pass 1: [title]Report[/title] has 42 items
28	After Pass 2: \x1b[1;36mReport\x1b[0m has 42 items  (or plain: "Report has 42 items")
29	```
30	
31	This separation means:
32	
33	- Template logic (loops, conditionals) is handled by MiniJinja—a mature, well-documented engine
34	- Style application is a simple, predictable transformation
35	- You can debug each pass independently
36	
37	---
38	
39	## MiniJinja Basics
40	
41	MiniJinja implements Jinja2 syntax, a widely-used templating language. Here's a quick overview:
42	
43	### Variables
44	
45	```jinja
46	{{ variable }}
47	{{ object.field }}
48	{{ list[0] }}
49	```
50	
51	### Control Flow
52	
53	```jinja
54	{% if condition %}
55	  Show this
56	{% elif other_condition %}
57	  Show that
58	{% else %}
59	  Default
60	{% endif %}
61	
62	{% for item in items %}
63	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	### Filters
68	
69	```jinja
70	{{ name | upper }}
71	{{ list | length }}
72	{{ value | default("N/A") }}
73	{{ text | truncate(20) }}
74	```
75	
76	### Comments
77	
78	```jinja
79	{# This is a comment and won't appear in output #}
80	```
81	
82	For comprehensive MiniJinja documentation, see the [MiniJinja documentation](https://docs.rs/minijinja).
83	
84	### Booleans and None
85	
86	Standout renders these the Rust way — `true`, `false`, `none` — not the Jinja2
87	way MiniJinja itself uses (`True`, `False`, `None`). This holds for
88	interpolation, loop and `set` bindings, `| string`, `| join`, sequence and map
89	literals, standout's own filters, and table cells:
90	
91	```jinja
92	{{ flag }}                {# true #}
93	{{ missing }}             {# none #}
94	{{ flags }}               {# [true, false, none] #}
95	{{ flags | join(", ") }}  {# true, false, none #}
96	```
97	
98	Two exceptions:
99	
100	- The `~` concatenation operator formats inside MiniJinja's evaluator, which
101	  exposes no hook: `{{ "x" ~ flag }}` yields `xTrue`. Write `{{ "x" }}{{ flag }}`
102	  or `{{ "x" ~ flag | string }}`.
103	- Structured output (JSON, YAML, XML, CSV) skips templates entirely and
104	  serializes your data directly, so those modes follow their format's own rules.
105	
106	If you build a `minijinja::Environment` yourself, use
107	`standout_render::template::new_environment()` — or call `register_filters` on
108	your own environment, which installs the same spelling.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## The Trailing-Newline Contract
113	
114	Two things happen to the newline at the end of a template, and together they
115	are observable in the bytes a script reads, so they are stated here rather than
116	discovered by probing.
117	
118	**The engine consumes exactly one final newline.** This is Jinja's rule and
119	MiniJinja keeps it. A template file ending in a single `\n` renders with no
120	trailing newline at all; a file ending in two renders with one.
121	
122	| Template source | Rendered string |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| `{{ name }}` | `x` |
125	| `{{ name }}\n` | `x` |
126	| `{{ name }}\n\n` | `x\n` |
127	| `{{ name }}\n\n\n` | `x\n\n` |
128	
129	**The process edge appends exactly one newline.** `App::run` writes a handled
130	command's text with `writeln!`, so what reaches stdout is the rendered string
131	plus one `\n` — whatever the template ended with.
132	
133	The practical consequence: a template that ends with one newline and a template
134	that ends with none produce identical bytes. To end a page with a blank line,
135	the template needs *two* trailing newlines. Every editor that adds a final
136	newline on save is therefore invisible here, which is the reason the rule is
137	worth stating.
138	
139	`standout-render/tests/trailing_newline.rs` pins the engine half;
140	`final_emission_routes_success_and_diagnostics_to_distinct_streams` in
141	`standout/src/cli/builder/execution.rs` pins the process half.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Style Tags
146	
147	Style tags use BBCode-like bracket notation to apply named styles from your theme:
148	
149	```jinja
150	[style-name]content to style[/style-name]
151	```
152	
153	### Basic Usage
154	
155	```jinja
156	[title]Report Summary[/title]
157	[error]Something went wrong![/error]
158	[muted]Last updated: {{ timestamp }}[/muted]
159	```
160	
161	### Nesting
162	
163	Tags can nest properly:
164	
165	```jinja
166	[outer][inner]nested content[/inner][/outer]
167	```
168	
169	### Spanning Lines
170	
171	Tags can span multiple lines:
172	
173	```jinja
174	[panel]
175	This is a multi-line
176	block of styled content
177	[/panel]
178	```
179	
180	### With Template Logic
181	
182	Style tags and MiniJinja work together seamlessly:
183	
184	```jinja
185	[title]{% if custom_title %}{{ custom_title }}{% else %}Default Title{% endif %}[/title]
186	
187	{% for task in tasks %}
188	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
189	{% endfor %}
190	```
191	
192	The second example shows dynamic style names—the style applied depends on the value of `task.status`.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Processing Modes
197	
198	Pass 2 (BBParser) processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
199	
200	| Mode | Behavior | Use Case |
201	| ------ | ---------- | ---------- |
202	| `Term` | Replace tags with ANSI escape codes | Rich terminal output |
203	| `Text` | Strip tags completely | Plain text, pipes, files |
204	| `TermDebug` | Keep tags as literal text | Debugging, testing |
205	
206	### Processing Modes Example
207	
208	Template: `[title]Hello[/title]`
209	
210	- **Term**: `\x1b[1;36mHello\x1b[0m` (rendered as cyan bold)
211	- **Text**: `Hello`
212	- **TermDebug**: `[title]Hello[/title]`
213	
214	### Setting the Mode
215	
216	```rust
217	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
218	
219	// Rich terminal
220	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
221	
222	// Plain text
223	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
224	
225	// Debug (tags visible)
226	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
227	
228	// Auto-detect based on TTY
229	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
230	```
231	
232	### Auto Mode
233	
234	`OutputMode::Auto` detects the appropriate mode:
235	
236	- If stdout is a TTY with color support → `Term`
237	- If stdout is a pipe or redirect → `Text`
238	
239	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` CLI flag automatically sets the output mode. See standout documentation for details.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Built-in Filters
244	
245	Beyond MiniJinja's standard filters, `standout-render` provides formatting filters:
246	
247	### Column Formatting
248	
249	```jinja
250	{{ value | col(10) }}                              {# pad/truncate to 10 chars #}
251	{{ value | col(20, align="right") }}               {# right-align in 20 chars #}
252	{{ value | col(15, truncate="middle") }}           {# truncate in middle #}
253	{{ value | col(15, truncate="start", ellipsis="...") }}
254	```
255	
256	### Padding
257	
258	```jinja
259	{{ "42" | pad_left(8) }}      {# "      42" #}
260	{{ "hi" | pad_right(8) }}     {# "hi      " #}
261	{{ "hi" | pad_center(8) }}    {# "   hi   " #}
262	```
263	
264	### Truncation
265	
266	```jinja
267	{{ long_text | truncate_at(20) }}                   {# "Very long text th..." #}
268	{{ path | truncate_at(30, "middle", "...") }}      {# "/home/.../file.txt" #}
269	{{ text | truncate_at(20, "start") }}              {# "...end of the text" #}
270	```
271	
272	### Display Width
273	
274	```jinja
275	{% if value | display_width > 20 %}
276	  {{ value | truncate_at(20) }}
277	{% else %}
278	  {{ value }}
279	{% endif %}
280	```
281	
282	Returns visual width (handles Unicode—CJK characters count as 2).
283	
284	### Style Application
285	
286	```jinja
287	{{ value | style_as("error") }}                    {# wraps in [error]...[/error] #}
288	{{ task.status | style_as(task.status) }}         {# dynamic: [pending]pending[/pending] #}
289	```
290	
291	---
292	
293	## Template Registry
294	
295	When using the `Renderer` struct, templates are resolved by name through a registry:
296	
297	```rust
298	use standout_render::Renderer;
299	
300	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
301	
302	// Add inline template
303	renderer.add_template("greeting", "Hello, [name]{{ name }}[/name]!")?;
304	
305	// Add directory of templates
306	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
307	
308	// Render by name
309	let output = renderer.render("greeting", &data)?;
310	```
311	
312	### Resolution Priority
313	
314	1. **Inline templates** (added via `add_template()`)
315	2. **Directory templates** (from `add_template_dir()`)
316	
317	### File Extensions
318	
319	Supported extensions (in priority order): `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`
320	
321	When you request `"report"`, the registry checks:
322	
323	- Inline template named `"report"`
324	- `report.jinja` in registered directories
325	- `report.jinja2`, `report.j2`, `report.stpl`, `report.txt` (lower priority)
326	
327	The `.stpl` extension is for SimpleEngine templates. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for details.
328	
329	### Template Names
330	
331	Template names are derived from relative paths:
332	
333	```text
334	templates/
335	├── greeting.jinja       → "greeting"
336	├── reports/
337	│   └── summary.jinja    → "reports/summary"
338	└── errors/
339	    └── 404.jinja        → "errors/404"
340	```
341	
342	---
343	
344	## Including Templates
345	
346	Templates can include other templates using MiniJinja's include syntax:
347	
348	```jinja
349	{# main.jinja #}
350	[title]{{ title }}[/title]
351	
352	{% include "partials/header.jinja" %}
353	
354	{% for item in items %}
355	  {% include "partials/item.jinja" %}
356	{% endfor %}
357	
358	{% include "partials/footer.jinja" %}
359	```
360	
361	This enables reusable components across your application.
362	
363	---
364	
365	## Context Variables
366	
367	Beyond your data, you can inject additional context into templates:
368	
369	```rust
370	use standout_render::{render_with_vars, OutputMode};
371	use std::collections::HashMap;
372	
373	let mut vars = HashMap::new();
374	vars.insert("version", "1.0.0");
375	vars.insert("app_name", "MyApp");
376	
377	let output = render_with_vars(
378	    "{{ app_name }} v{{ version }}: {{ message }}",
379	    &data,
380	    &theme,
381	    OutputMode::Term,
382	    vars,
383	)?;
384	```
385	
386	When handler data and context variables have the same key, **handler data wins**. Context is supplementary.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## Structured Output
391	
392	For machine-readable output (JSON, YAML, CSV), templates are bypassed entirely:
393	
394	```rust
395	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
396	
397	// Template is used for Term/Text modes
398	// Data is serialized directly for Json/Yaml/Csv
399	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
400	```
401	
402	| Mode | Behavior |
403	| ------ | ---------- |
404	| `Term` | Render template, apply styles |
405	| `Text` | Render template, strip styles |
406	| `TermDebug` | Render template, keep style tags |
407	| `Json` | `serde_json::to_string_pretty(data)` |
408	| `Yaml` | `serde_yaml::to_string(data)` |
409	| `Csv` | Flatten and format as CSV |
410	
411	This means your serializable data types automatically support structured output without additional code.
412	
413	---
414	
415	## Validation
416	
417	Check templates for unknown style tags before deploying:
418	
419	```rust
420	use standout_render::validate_template;
421	
422	let errors = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme);
423	if !errors.is_empty() {
424	    for error in &errors {
425	        eprintln!("Unknown style tag: [{}]", error.tag_name);
426	    }
427	}
428	```
429	
430	Validation catches:
431	
432	- Misspelled style names
433	- References to undefined styles
434	- Mismatched opening/closing tags
435	
436	---
437	
438	## API Reference
439	
440	### Render Functions
441	
442	```rust
443	use standout_render::{
444	    render,                  // Basic: template + data + theme
445	    render_with_output,      // With explicit output mode
446	    render_with_mode,        // With output mode + color mode
447	    render_with_vars,        // With extra context variables
448	    render_auto,             // Auto-dispatch template vs serialize
449	    render_auto_with_context,
450	};
451	
452	// Basic
453	let output = render(template, &data, &theme)?;
454	
455	// With output mode
456	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
457	
458	// With color mode override (for testing)
459	let output = render_with_mode(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term, ColorMode::Dark)?;
460	
461	// Auto (template for text modes, serialize for structured)
462	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
463	```
464	
465	### Renderer Struct
466	
467	```rust
468	use standout_render::Renderer;
469	
470	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
471	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
472	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
473	
474	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
475	let output = renderer.render_with_mode("name", &data, OutputMode::Text)?;
476	```

1	# The `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` Reference
2	
3	Two macros carry the blessed idiom. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` on an enum binds
4	command names to handler functions; `#[handler]` on a function turns it into
5	something the dispatcher can call. This page is the complete list of what each
6	one accepts.
7	
8	Both name mappings on this page — a variant name to a command name, and a
9	parameter name to a clap argument id — are contract, because they decide the
10	words a user types in a shell script. See
11	[What Is Contract](stability.md#4-the-two-name-mappings-a-user-types-on-the-command-line).
12	
13	## `#[derive(Dispatch)]`
14	
15	### The container attribute
16	
17	One attribute goes on the enum, and it is required:
18	
19	```rust,ignore
20	#[derive(Dispatch)]
21	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
22	enum Commands { /* … */ }
23	```
24	
25	`handlers = <module path>` names the module the derive looks each variant's
26	handler up in. Without it, expansion fails with `missing #[dispatch(handlers =
27	path)] attribute`.
28	
29	### From a variant name to a command name
30	
31	A variant registers under its **kebab-case** name — `ListUnits` becomes
32	`list-units` — which is the spelling clap's own derive gives the subcommand.
33	`#[dispatch(name = "…")]` renames one variant.
34	
35	A `name` may not be empty and may not contain `.`: dispatch splits registration
36	paths on `.`, so such a name would register a nested path no clap subcommand
37	declares. Nesting is `#[dispatch(nested)]`, below.
38	
39	A registered path that no clap subcommand can reach is a loud error naming the
40	path, raised by `App::run` and `App::verify_command` before dispatch.
41	
42	### From a variant name to a handler function
43	
44	The handler is looked up under the variant's **snake_case** name in the
45	`handlers` module — `ListUnits` calls `handlers::list_units`. Two attributes
46	change that:
47	
48	- `#[dispatch(pure)]` appends `__handler`, so the derive calls
49	  `handlers::list_units__handler` — the wrapper `#[handler]` generated. Use it
50	  whenever the handler function carries `#[handler]`, which is the blessed
51	  style. The derive registers through a closure taking `HandlerResult<T>`, so a
52	  `pure` handler must be annotated `-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or
53	  `-> Result<(), E>`; a plain `-> Result<T, E>` fails expansion. See
54	  [what `#[handler]` generates](#what-handler-generates).
55	- `#[dispatch(handler = <path>)]` names the function outright and ignores the
56	  inferred name.
57	
58	The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
59	naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
60	that function must already have the dispatch signature.
61	
62	### Every variant attribute
63	
64	Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
65	anything reads them.
66	
67	| Attribute | Form | What it does |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
70	| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
71	| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
72	| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
73	| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
74	| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
75	| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
76	| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
77	| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
78	| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
79	| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
80	| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
81	| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
82	| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
83	| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
84	| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
85	| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
86	| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
87	| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
88	| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |
89	
90	An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.
91	
92	### Nested commands
93	
94	`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:
95	
96	```rust,ignore
97	#[derive(Dispatch)]
98	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
99	enum Commands {
100	    #[dispatch(nested)]
101	    Pr(PrCommands),
102	}
103	```
104	
105	The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
106	variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
107	recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.
108	
109	### How a command finds its template
110	
111	With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
112	`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
113	`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:
114	
115	| Registration path | Template name |
116	| --- | --- |
117	| `list` | `list` |
118	| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |
119	
120	The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
121	`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
122	command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
123	looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
124	name retried.
125	
126	`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
127	choose, which is how two commands share one template.
128	
129	## `#[handler]`
130	
131	### Parameter attributes
132	
133	Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
134	macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
135	reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
136	needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.
137	
138	| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
141	| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
142	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
143	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
144	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
145	| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |
146	
147	### From a parameter name to a clap argument id
148	
149	**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
150	argument whose id is `no-legend`.
151	
152	Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
153	disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:
154	
155	```rust,ignore
156	#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
157	no_legend: bool,
158	
159	#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
160	no_legend: bool,
161	```
162	
163	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
164	leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.
165	
166	A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
167	derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.
168	
169	### What `#[handler]` generates
170	
171	For `fn list`, four items:
172	
173	| Item | What it is |
174	| --- | --- |
175	| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
176	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
177	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
178	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |
179	
180	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
181	not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
182	accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
183	`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
184	`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
185	takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
186	`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
187	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
188	`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.
189	
190	See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
191	the return types themselves.
192	
193	## A worked example
194	
195	Every attribute below is exercised by
196	`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
197	`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.
198	
199	```rust
200	use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
201	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
202	use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};
203	
204	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
205	pub struct Units {
206	    pub names: Vec<String>,
207	}
208	
209	pub mod handlers {
210	    use super::*;
211	
212	    #[handler]
213	    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
214	        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
215	        if all {
216	            names.push("cron".to_string());
217	        }
218	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
219	    }
220	
221	    #[handler]
222	    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
223	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
224	    }
225	
226	    #[handler]
227	    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
228	        Ok(())
229	    }
230	}
231	
232	#[derive(Dispatch)]
233	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
234	pub enum Commands {
235	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
236	    ListUnits,
237	    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
238	    About,
239	    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
240	    Reload,
241	}
242	
243	const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
244	    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
245	    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
246	];
247	
248	/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
249	/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
250	/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
251	fn command() -> Command {
252	    Command::new("unitctl")
253	        .subcommand(
254	            Command::new("list-units")
255	                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
256	        )
257	        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
258	        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
259	}
260	
261	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
262	    let app: App = App::builder()
263	        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
264	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
265	        .build()?;
266	    app.verify_command(&command())?;
267	    Ok(())
268	}
269	```
270	
271	`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
272	`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
273	runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
274	`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
275	reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
276	the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
277	entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
278	convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
279	`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.

# The `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` Reference

Two macros carry the blessed idiom. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` on an enum binds
command names to handler functions; `#[handler]` on a function turns it into
something the dispatcher can call. This page is the complete list of what each
one accepts.

Both name mappings on this page — a variant name to a command name, and a
parameter name to a clap argument id — are contract, because they decide the
words a user types in a shell script. See
[What Is Contract](stability.md#4-the-two-name-mappings-a-user-types-on-the-command-line).

## `#[derive(Dispatch)]`

### The container attribute

One attribute goes on the enum, and it is required:

```rust,ignore
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands { /* … */ }
```

`handlers = <module path>` names the module the derive looks each variant's
handler up in. Without it, expansion fails with `missing #[dispatch(handlers =
path)] attribute`.

### From a variant name to a command name

A variant registers under its **kebab-case** name — `ListUnits` becomes
`list-units` — which is the spelling clap's own derive gives the subcommand.
`#[dispatch(name = "…")]` renames one variant.

A `name` may not be empty and may not contain `.`: dispatch splits registration
paths on `.`, so such a name would register a nested path no clap subcommand
declares. Nesting is `#[dispatch(nested)]`, below.

A registered path that no clap subcommand can reach is a loud error naming the
path, raised by `App::run` and `App::verify_command` before dispatch.

### From a variant name to a handler function

The handler is looked up under the variant's **snake_case** name in the
`handlers` module — `ListUnits` calls `handlers::list_units`. Two attributes
change that:

- `#[dispatch(pure)]` appends `__handler`, so the derive calls
  `handlers::list_units__handler` — the wrapper `#[handler]` generated. Use it
  whenever the handler function carries `#[handler]`, which is the blessed
  style. The derive registers through a closure taking `HandlerResult<T>`, so a
  `pure` handler must be annotated `-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or
  `-> Result<(), E>`; a plain `-> Result<T, E>` fails expansion. See
  [what `#[handler]` generates](#what-handler-generates).
- `#[dispatch(handler = <path>)]` names the function outright and ignores the
  inferred name.

The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
that function must already have the dispatch signature.

### Every variant attribute

Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
anything reads them.

| Attribute | Form | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |

An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.

### Nested commands

`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:

```rust,ignore
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(nested)]
    Pr(PrCommands),
}
```

The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.

### How a command finds its template

With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:

| Registration path | Template name |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | `list` |
| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |

The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
name retried.

`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
choose, which is how two commands share one template.

## `#[handler]`

### Parameter attributes

Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.

| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |

### From a parameter name to a clap argument id

**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
argument whose id is `no-legend`.

Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:

```rust,ignore
#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
no_legend: bool,

#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
no_legend: bool,
```

`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.

A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.

### What `#[handler]` generates

For `fn list`, four items:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.

See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
the return types themselves.

## A worked example

Every attribute below is exercised by
`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.

```rust
use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Units {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

pub mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    #[handler]
    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
        if all {
            names.push("cron".to_string());
        }
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
pub enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
    ListUnits,
    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
    About,
    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
    Reload,
}

const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
];

/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
fn command() -> Command {
    Command::new("unitctl")
        .subcommand(
            Command::new("list-units")
                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
        )
        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let app: App = App::builder()
        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
        .build()?;
    app.verify_command(&command())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.

1	# The Styling System
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a theme-based styling system where named styles are applied to content through bracket notation tags. Instead of embedding ANSI codes in your templates, you define semantic style names (`error`, `title`, `muted`) and let the theme decide the visual representation.
4	
5	This separation provides several benefits:
6	
7	- **Readability**: Templates use meaningful names, not escape codes
8	- **Maintainability**: Change colors in one place, update everywhere
9	- **Adaptability**: Themes can respond to light/dark mode automatically
10	- **Consistency**: Enforce visual hierarchy across your application
11	
12	---
13	
14	## Themes
15	
16	A `Theme` is a named collection of styles. Each style maps a name (like `title` or `error`) to visual attributes (bold cyan, dim red, etc.).
17	
18	### CSS Themes
19	
20	Define styles in standard CSS syntax — a subset of CSS Level 3 tailored for terminals:
21	
22	```css
23	/* theme.css */
24	.title {
25	    color: cyan;
26	    font-weight: bold;
27	}
28	
29	.error {
30	    color: red;
31	    font-weight: bold;
32	}
33	
34	.muted {
35	    opacity: 0.5;  /* maps to dim */
36	}
37	
38	.success {
39	    color: green;
40	}
41	
42	/* Shorthand works too */
43	.warning { color: yellow; }
44	```
45	
46	Load CSS themes:
47	
48	```rust
49	use standout_render::Theme;
50	
51	let theme = Theme::from_css(css_content)?;
52	```
53	
54	`Theme` parses a CSS string; reading the file is the caller's job:
55	
56	```rust
57	let css = std::fs::read_to_string("styles/theme.css")?;
58	let theme = Theme::from_css(&css)?;
59	```
60	
61	For a whole directory of themes with hot reload in debug builds, use
62	`AppBuilder::styles_dir` (see [App Configuration](../../../topics/app-configuration.md))
63	rather than reading a single file.
64	
65	CSS gives you syntax highlighting in editors, linting tools, and familiarity for web developers.
66	
67	### Programmatic Themes
68	
69	Build themes in code using the builder pattern:
70	
71	```rust
72	use standout_render::Theme;
73	use console::Style;
74	
75	let theme = Theme::new()
76	    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
77	    .add("error", Style::new().red().bold())
78	    .add("muted", Style::new().dim())
79	    .add("success", Style::new().green());
80	```
81	
82	> **Legacy format:** YAML themes are still supported via `Theme::from_yaml()`. CSS is the recommended format for all new projects.
83	
84	---
85	
86	## Supported Attributes
87	
88	### Colors
89	
90	| Attribute | CSS Property | Description             |
91	| --------- | ------------ | ----------------------- |
92	| `fg`      | `color`      | Foreground (text) color |
93	| `bg`      | `background` | Background color        |
94	
95	### Color Formats
96	
97	```css
98	/* Named colors (16 ANSI colors) */
99	.example { color: red; }
100	.example { color: green; }
101	.example { color: cyan; }
102	.example { color: magenta; }
103	.example { color: yellow; }
104	.example { color: white; }
105	.example { color: black; }
106	
107	/* Bright variants */
108	.example { color: bright_red; }
109	.example { color: bright_green; }
110	
111	/* 256-color palette (0-255) */
112	.example { color: 208; }
113	
114	/* RGB hex */
115	.example { color: #ff6b35; }
116	.example { color: #f63; }     /* shorthand */
117	
118	/* Theme-relative cube colors */
119	.example { color: cube(60%, 20%, 0%); }
120	```
121	
122	Cube colors express a position in a color cube whose 8 corners are the base ANSI
123	colors of the user's terminal theme. The same `cube(60%, 20%, 0%)` produces earthy
124	tones in Gruvbox, pastels in Catppuccin, and muted shades in Solarized.
125	Interpolation is done in CIE LAB space for perceptually uniform gradients.
126	Attach a palette to a theme with `Theme::with_palette()`.
127	
128	### Text Attributes
129	
130	| CSS Property                    | Effect            |
131	| ------------------------------- | ----------------- |
132	| `font-weight: bold`             | Bold text         |
133	| `opacity: 0.5`                  | Dimmed/faint text |
134	| `font-style: italic`            | Italic text       |
135	| `text-decoration: underline`    | Underlined text   |
136	| `text-decoration: blink`        | Blinking text     |
137	| `text-decoration: line-through` | Strikethrough     |
138	| `visibility: hidden`            | Hidden text       |
139	
140	---
141	
142	## Adaptive Styles (Light/Dark Mode)
143	
144	Terminal applications run in both light and dark environments. A color that looks great on a dark background may be illegible on a light one. `standout-render` solves this with adaptive styles.
145	
146	### How It Works
147	
148	Instead of defining separate "light theme" and "dark theme" files, you define mode-specific overrides at the style level:
149	
150	```css
151	.panel {
152	    font-weight: bold;
153	    color: gray;        /* Default/fallback */
154	}
155	
156	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
157	    .panel { color: black; }   /* Override for light mode */
158	}
159	
160	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
161	    .panel { color: white; }   /* Override for dark mode */
162	}
163	```
164	
165	When resolving `panel` in dark mode:
166	
167	1. Start with base attributes (`bold`, `gray`)
168	2. Merge dark overrides (`white` replaces `gray`)
169	3. Result: bold white text
170	
171	This is efficient: most styles (bold, italic, semantic colors like green/red) look fine in both modes. Only a handful need adjustment—typically foreground colors for contrast.
172	
173	### Programmatic API
174	
175	```rust
176	use standout_render::Theme;
177	use console::{Style, Color};
178	
179	let theme = Theme::new()
180	    .add_adaptive(
181	        "panel",
182	        Style::new().bold(),                     // Base (shared)
183	        Some(Style::new().fg(Color::Black)),     // Light mode
184	        Some(Style::new().fg(Color::White)),     // Dark mode
185	    );
186	```
187	
188	### Color Mode Detection
189	
190	`standout-render` auto-detects the OS color scheme when the caller probes the process:
191	
192	```rust
193	use standout_render::{ColorMode, TargetProperties};
194	
195	let properties = TargetProperties::detect();
196	match properties.color_scheme {
197	    ColorMode::Light => println!("Light mode"),
198	    ColorMode::Dark => println!("Dark mode"),
199	}
200	```
201	
202	`TargetProperties::detect()` is the one process probe, at the crate edge. Convenience wrappers call it then pass the result into `render_request`. Tests construct `TargetProperties` with an explicit `color_scheme` rather than installing a detector; `set_theme_detector` and the other detector override APIs are removed.
203	
204	---
205	
206	## Style Aliasing
207	
208	Aliases let semantic names resolve to visual styles. This is useful when multiple concepts share the same appearance:
209	
210	```rust
211	let theme = Theme::new()
212	    // Define the visual style once
213	    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
214	    // Aliases — pass a string to reference another style by name
215	    .add("commit-message", "title")
216	    .add("section-header", "title")
217	    .add("heading", "title");
218	```
219	
220	Now `[commit-message]`, `[section-header]`, and `[heading]` all render identically to `[title]`.
221	
222	Benefits:
223	
224	- Templates use meaningful, context-specific names
225	- Visual changes propagate automatically
226	- Refactoring visual design doesn't touch templates
227	
228	Aliases can chain: `a` → `b` → `c` → concrete style. Cycles are detected and rejected at load time.
229	
230	---
231	
232	## Unknown Style Tags
233	
234	When a template references a style not defined in the theme, `standout-render` handles it gracefully:
235	
236	| Output Mode | Behavior                                                   |
237	| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
238	| `Term`      | Unknown tags get a `?` marker: `[unknown?]text[/unknown?]` |
239	| `Text`      | Tags stripped (plain text)                                 |
240	| `TermDebug` | Tags preserved as-is                                       |
241	
242	The `?` marker helps catch typos during development without crashing production apps.
243	
244	### Validation
245	
246	For strict checking at startup:
247	
248	```rust
249	use standout_render::validate_template;
250	
251	if let Err(error) = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme) {
252	    eprintln!("Unknown style tag: {}", error);
253	    std::process::exit(1);
254	}
255	```
256	
257	---
258	
259	## Built-in Styles
260	
261	`Theme::default()` includes adaptive styles for alternating table row backgrounds. These are used automatically when you pass `row_styles=true` (or a tint name) to the `table()` template function.
262	
263	| Style name              | Purpose                                 |
264	| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
265	| `table_row_even`        | Even rows — no background (transparent) |
266	| `table_row_odd`         | Odd rows — subtle gray background shift |
267	| `table_row_even_gray`   | Alias for `table_row_even`              |
268	| `table_row_odd_gray`    | Alias for `table_row_odd`               |
269	| `table_row_even_blue`   | Even rows for blue tint                 |
270	| `table_row_odd_blue`    | Odd rows — dark navy / lavender bg      |
271	| `table_row_even_red`    | Even rows for red tint                  |
272	| `table_row_odd_red`     | Odd rows — dark crimson / blush bg      |
273	| `table_row_even_green`  | Even rows for green tint                |
274	| `table_row_odd_green`   | Odd rows — dark forest / mint bg        |
275	| `table_row_even_purple` | Even rows for purple tint               |
276	| `table_row_odd_purple`  | Odd rows — dark plum / lilac bg         |
277	
278	All odd-row styles are adaptive: they resolve to a dark variant when the terminal is in dark mode, and a light variant in light mode. You can override any of these by defining the same style name in your theme.
279	
280	---
281	
282	## Best Practices
283	
284	### Semantic, Presentation, and Visual Layers
285	
286	Organize your styles in three conceptual layers:
287	
288	**1. Visual primitives** (low-level appearance):
289	
290	```css
291	._cyan-bold { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
292	._dim { opacity: 0.5; }
293	._red-bold { color: red; font-weight: bold; }
294	```
295	
296	**2. Presentation roles** (UI concepts — use aliases in code):
297	
298	```rust
299	theme.add("heading", "_cyan-bold")
300	     .add("secondary", "_dim")
301	     .add("danger", "_red-bold");
302	```
303	
304	**3. Semantic names** (domain concepts — aliases to presentation):
305	
306	```rust
307	// In templates, use these
308	theme.add("task-title", "heading")
309	     .add("task-status-done", "success")
310	     .add("task-status-pending", "warning")
311	     .add("error-message", "danger");
312	```
313	
314	Templates use semantic names (`task-title`), which resolve to presentation roles (`heading`), which resolve to visual primitives (`_cyan-bold`).
315	
316	This layering lets you:
317	
318	- Refactor visuals without touching templates
319	- Maintain consistency across domains
320	- Document the purpose of each style
321	
322	### Naming Conventions
323	
324	```css
325	/* Good: descriptive, semantic */
326	.error-message { ... }
327	.file-path { ... }
328	.command-name { ... }
329	
330	/* Avoid: visual descriptions */
331	.red-text { ... }
332	.bold-cyan { ... }
333	```
334	
335	### Keep Themes Focused
336	
337	One theme per "look". Don't mix concerns:
338	
339	```text
340	styles/
341	├── default.css          # your app's default look
342	├── colorblind.css       # accessibility variant
343	└── monochrome.css       # for piped output
344	```
345	
346	---
347	
348	## API Reference
349	
350	### Theme Creation
351	
352	```rust
353	// From CSS string
354	let theme = Theme::from_css(css_str)?;
355	
356	// Empty theme (for programmatic building)
357	let theme = Theme::new();
358	
359	// Legacy: YAML is still supported
360	let theme = Theme::from_yaml(yaml_str)?;
361	```
362	
363	### Adding Styles
364	
365	```rust
366	// Static style
367	theme.add("name", Style::new().bold());
368	
369	// Adaptive style
370	theme.add_adaptive("name", base_style, light_override, dark_override);
371	
372	// Alias
373	theme.add("alias", "target_style");
374	```
375	
376	### Resolving Styles
377	
378	```rust
379	// Get the mode-agnostic style
380	let style: Option<Style> = theme.get_style("title", None);
381	
382	// Get style resolved for a specific mode
383	let style = theme.get_style("panel", Some(ColorMode::Dark));
384	```
385	
386	### Color Mode
387	
388	```rust
389	use standout_render::{ColorMode, TargetProperties};
390	
391	// Auto-detect at the crate edge
392	let properties = TargetProperties::detect();
393	let mode = properties.color_scheme;
394	
395	// Tests construct TargetProperties instead of installing a detector
396	let mut target = properties;
397	target.color_scheme = ColorMode::Light;
398	```

input.command:
cd "[workspace]/.tmptest" && B=$PWD/../app/target/debug/gitlike
ref=$($B ref-list | od -c | md5)
for mode in auto term text term-debug json yaml xml csv; do
  for env in "" "NO_COLOR=1" "GITLIKE_THEME=mono" "GITLIKE_PAGER=cat" "PAGER=cat"; do
    got=$(env $env $B ref-list --output $mode | od -c | md5)
    [ "$got" = "$ref" ] || echo "MISMATCH ref-list mode=$mode env=$env"
  done
done
co=$($B cat-object c1a9 | od -c | md5)
for mode in auto term text term-debug json yaml xml csv; do
  got=$($B cat-object c1a9 --output $mode | od -c | md5)
  [ "$got" = "$co" ] || echo "MISMATCH cat-object mode=$mode"
done
echo "plumbing stability checked"
echo "== cat-object unknown across modes =="
for mode in auto term json; do $B cat-object nope --output $mode 2>&1 1>/dev/null; echo "  mode=$mode exit=$?"; done
echo "== log --limit 2 =="; $B log --limit 2

#! standout-answers 1
#! questionnaire: corpus.exit
#! fingerprint: sha256:64291870245510dad73ca960fd4024db9b9c161113a3dcc9c7e57a30973663fc

1. Summarize what you built and what state it is in. (text) <id:summary>

`gitlike`, complete and building clean (`cargo build`, no warnings from my
code), with every command in SPEC.md verified by running the binary.

Structure in `app/src/`:

- `repo.rs` — the frozen three-commit / two-branch state, as consts.
- `config.rs` — the two config keys, resolved from the nearest `.gitlike.toml`
  walking up from the cwd, then `$GITLIKE_CONFIG_HOME/config.toml` (else
  `$HOME/.config/gitlike/config.toml`). Precedence is per key: the repo file
  wins for the keys it sets, the user file fills the rest. Both TOML spellings
  (`log.limit = 2` and `[log] limit = 2`) work, because the toml crate
  normalizes dotted keys.
- `cli.rs` — clap derive plus `#[derive(Dispatch)]`. `log` and `status` are
  `#[dispatch(pure)]`; the plumbing variants are `#[dispatch(skip)]`.
- `handlers.rs` — the two porcelain `#[handler]` adapters returning view data.
- `templates/log.jinja`, `templates/status.jinja`, `styles/default.css`,
  `styles/mono.css`.
- `plumbing.rs` — `ref-list`, `cat-object` and `config get`, registered with
  `command_passthrough`. That was the deliberate design choice for the
  stability contract: a passthrough handler writes its own bytes and, per
  `docs/topics/passthrough.md`, `--output` has no way to reach it, so the
  plumbing bytes are identical under every theme, every `--output` mode and
  terminal or pipe. I verified that as a matrix (8 output modes × 5
  environments for `ref-list`, 8 modes for `cat-object`) — all byte-identical.
- `pager.rs` — paging, which the framework does not provide for command output
  (only for help/topics). Porcelain pages when stdout is a terminal, the
  invocation did not pass `--no-pager`, and `GITLIKE_PAGER` (else `PAGER`)
  names a non-blank command, which is run through `sh -c`.
- `main.rs` — `App::builder()` wiring plus `run_with`, because the process edge
  had to be mine to page: `run()` performs the final write itself. `main` does
  what `run()` documents — one trailing newline via `writeln!`, diagnostics to
  stderr, the framework's own exit status — and routes porcelain text through
  the pager plan instead of straight to stdout.

Theme selection reads `GITLIKE_THEME` at build time and feeds
`.default_theme("mono"|"default")`. `NO_COLOR` and pipe-vs-terminal are the
framework's `auto` mode doing its documented job; I add nothing there.

Exit codes verified: 0 success, 1 `config get` on an unset key (silent on both
streams), 2 unknown command / unknown flag / `--limit 0` / missing argument,
3 unknown object hash (with `gitlike: no such object: <hash>` on stderr).

2. Which of the provided documentation files (under docs/) did you actually consult? List their paths. (text) <id:sources.docs>

- docs/index.md
- docs/guides/intro-to-standout.md
- docs/topics/index.md
- docs/topics/stability.md
- docs/topics/app-configuration.md
- docs/topics/output-modes.md
- docs/topics/execution-outcomes.md
- docs/topics/error-handling.md
- docs/topics/passthrough.md
- docs/topics/seeker.md
- docs/topics/topics-system.md
- docs/topics/dispatch-attributes.md
- docs/crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md
- docs/crates/render/topics/templating.md
- docs/crates/render/topics/styling-system.md

I also grepped the whole `docs/` tree for `pager`/`paging`, `NO_COLOR`,
`plumbing`/`porcelain` and `page` to find out whether the framework owned any
of those; that is how I established that paging exists only for help and
topics, not for command output.

3. Did you rely on anything beyond the provided docs/ — web search, prior knowledge of standout internals, other repositories or source code? Say exactly what, or answer 'none'. (text) <id:sources.external>

No web search, no standout source, no other repositories. Two things came from
outside the prose in `docs/`:

- Rust and crate general knowledge: clap 4 derive, serde, the `toml` crate
  (which I added to `app/Cargo.toml`), `std::io::IsTerminal`, and
  `std::process::Command` for the pager.
- The compiler, used as an API oracle where `docs/` was wrong or silent. When
  `use standout::cli::AppFailure` failed to resolve I probed nearby paths
  (`standout::AppFailure`, `standout::dispatch::AppFailure`,
  `standout_dispatch::AppFailure`) and a deliberate typo
  (`standout::cli::ExternalFailur`) to make rustc's "a similar name exists"
  suggestion tell me what the module actually exports. That is compiler
  feedback on my own crate, not reading standout's source, but it is knowledge
  the docs did not give me. `ExitStatus::code()` and the `&self` receivers on
  `App::get_matches_from` / `App::run_with` were likewise confirmed by
  compiling rather than by reading a doc.

4. Friction points, if any: for each, quote the exact command, error message, or doc passage that caused it. (text, optional) <id:friction>

a) `AppFailure` does not exist. `docs/topics/error-handling.md` says:

    use standout::cli::{AppFailure, HandlerResult};
    ...
    return Err(AppFailure::new(1, "ghlike: repository not found: demo/gamma\n")?.into());

and `docs/crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md` repeats it. The build says:

    error[E0432]: unresolved import `standout::cli::AppFailure`
      --> src/plumbing.rs:11:21
       |
    11 | use standout::cli::{AppFailure, CommandContext};
       |                     ^^^^^^^^^^ no `AppFailure` in `cli`

`standout::AppFailure` and `standout_dispatch::AppFailure` fail the same way,
and rustc offers no similar-name suggestion, so nothing close to that spelling
is exported. `ExternalFailure` *is* there — rustc suggested it when I misspelled
it — so I used that instead. See the workarounds answer.

b) No paging seam for command output. The only paging in `docs/` is
`docs/topics/topics-system.md` ("For long topics, the `--page` flag displays
content through a pager") and `docs/topics/standout-help.md` ("paging is a
terminal side effect and only a *printing* entry point may perform it"). Since
SPEC.md requires porcelain commands to page, and `run()` owns the final write,
I had to move to `run_with` and re-implement the process edge. That is a
documented capture path, but it means re-deriving behavior `run()` gets for
free (the trailing newline, the stderr split, the exit status).

c) Getting the trailing newline right needed care.
`docs/crates/render/topics/templating.md#the-trailing-newline-contract` says
the engine eats one final newline and "`App::run` writes a handled command's
text with `writeln!`". A naive `{% for %}` loop whose body ends in a newline
therefore renders with a trailing newline *and* gets one appended, producing a
blank last line. I wrote the loop's separator as
`{% if not loop.last %}<newline>{% endif %}` so the rendered string ends
without a newline, matching what `writeln!` expects.

d) Writing an "unstyled" theme is not obvious. `docs/crates/render/topics/styling-system.md`
says an undefined tag in `Term` mode gets a marker: "Unknown tags get a `?`
marker: `[unknown?]text[/unknown?]`". So `mono` could not simply omit the
styles — it has to define every tag with a declaration that resolves to no
attributes. I used `opacity: 1` (the doc only documents `opacity: 0.5` as
dim) and verified with `GITLIKE_THEME=mono gitlike log --output term` that the
bytes are plain, with no ANSI and no `?` markers.

5. Places the documentation was wrong or missing, if any: quote what the doc says and what actually happened. (text, optional) <id:docs.gaps>

- Wrong: `AppFailure`. Quoted in the friction answer — the docs give it an
  import path, a constructor signature and two worked examples, and the symbol
  is not in standout 9.0.0 under any path I could reach.
  `docs/topics/stability.md` even lists it as contract ("that is `AppFailure`,
  and `ExternalFailure` for a status another operation declared").

- Missing: whether owner-declared failures work from a *passthrough* handler.
  `docs/topics/passthrough.md` says only "the `anyhow::Error` becomes the
  command's failure", and `docs/topics/error-handling.md` frames both failure
  types as reached "through the same `HandlerResult` seam" — which passthrough
  does not use. It does work (`gitlike cat-object nosuch` exits 3 with the
  exact stderr line, `gitlike config get log.limit` exits 1 silently), but I
  found that out by running it, not by reading it.

- Missing: `ExitStatus`'s accessor. `docs/topics/execution-outcomes.md` shows
  `assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS))` but never says
  how a printing caller turns that into a process status. `.code()` returning
  `u8` was a guess that compiled.

- Missing: whether `App::get_matches_from` / `App::run_with` take `&self`.
  Both do, so one `App` can be parsed against and then run; the docs' examples
  never show both on the same value, and I had `let mut app` until the
  unused-`mut` warning told me otherwise.

- Missing: paging for command output, covered in the friction answer.
  `docs/topics/output-modes.md` mentions `myapp list | less` only as an example
  of color detection, never as something the framework can drive.

6. Workarounds you left in the produced code, if any. (text, optional) <id:workarounds>

- `src/plumbing.rs` uses `ExternalFailure` where the docs' blessed seam is
  `AppFailure`. Semantically `ExternalFailure` is documented for "relaying a
  verdict" another executable reached, which `gitlike` is not doing; I use it
  purely because it is the surviving type with the required shape (nonzero
  status + verbatim stderr payload, no framing). A comment above the import
  says so. If `AppFailure` reappears, swapping the two names is the whole fix.

- `src/main.rs` uses `run_with` rather than the blessed `run`, and
  reimplements the final write, so that porcelain can be paged. The cost is
  that framework warnings are dropped: `run()` flushes them to stderr, and
  capture runs drain them instead. `gitlike` produces none, but I do not
  forward `result.warnings()`, so a future one would be silent.

- `src/pager.rs` parses the command line twice — once via
  `app.get_matches_from(...)` to learn whether the invocation is porcelain and
  whether `--no-pager` was passed, then again inside `run_with`. Paging has to
  be decided before dispatch and there is no hook that reports the resolved
  command to the caller ahead of the run.

- The pager is run through `sh -c`, so `PAGER="less -R"` works. A pager
  command that does not exist is a successfully-spawned shell that then fails,
  which means that invocation's output is lost (as it is with git). Only a
  shell that will not start at all falls back to stdout.

- Malformed config is treated as absent rather than as an error: an
  unparseable `.gitlike.toml`, a non-integer `log.limit`, or a non-positive
  one all resolve to "unset". SPEC.md's exit-code table enumerates 0/1/2/3 and
  has no status for a bad config file, so I kept the tool inside that set
  rather than inventing one.

7. How confident are you that the acceptance criteria in SPEC.md pass? (low, medium, or high) <id:confidence>

medium-high, with one honest gap.

Verified by running the binary: all four command outputs byte-for-byte
(checked with `od -c`), all four exit codes, the `cat-object` stderr line,
`config get` silence-and-1 on an unset key, `--limit` overriding the config,
config precedence across `.gitlike.toml` at two depths plus
`$GITLIKE_CONFIG_HOME` and the `$HOME` fallback, and plumbing byte-stability
across the full `--output` × environment matrix.

The gap: this sandbox has no pty devices (`script` gives "openpty: Operation
not permitted", Python's `pty.openpty()` gives "out of pty devices"), so I
could not run the binary with a real terminal on stdout. I tested the paging
machinery by temporarily forcing the terminal check to pass — pager selection,
`GITLIKE_PAGER` beating `PAGER`, a blank variable, `--no-pager` in both
positions, plumbing refusing to page, and the fallback — then removed the
override. What remains unverified end-to-end is the `is_terminal()` gate
itself, and the framework-owned half of the terminal path: that `auto` really
resolves to `term` on a tty and that `NO_COLOR` really suppresses it. Both are
documented framework behavior I do not touch, but I did not see them run.

blank last line. I wrote the loop's separator as

without a newline, matching what `writeln!` expects.

  exact stderr line, `gitlike config get log.limit` exits 1 silently), but I

  `u8` was a guess that compiled.

  never show both on the same value, and I had `let mut app` until the
  unused-`mut` warning told me otherwise.

  verdict" another executable reached, which `gitlike` is not doing; I use it
  purely because it is the surviving type with the required shape (nonzero
  status + verbatim stderr payload, no framing). A comment above the import
  says so. If `AppFailure` reappears, swapping the two names is the whole fix.

  reimplements the final write, so that porcelain can be paged. The cost is

  whether `--no-pager` was passed, then again inside `run_with`. Paging has to

  command to the caller ahead of the run.

  command that does not exist is a successfully-spawned shell that then fails,
  which means that invocation's output is lost (as it is with git). Only a
  shell that will not start at all falls back to stdout.

  unparseable `.gitlike.toml`, a non-integer `log.limit`, or a non-positive
  one all resolve to "unset". SPEC.md's exit-code table enumerates 0/1/2/3 and
  has no status for a bad config file, so I kept the tool inside that set
  rather than inventing one.

Done. `gitlike` is built, running, and the questionnaire is filled in.

## What I built

`app/src/` — porcelain and plumbing are deliberately different registration shapes:

| Surface | Commands | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Porcelain | `log`, `status` | `#[derive(Dispatch)]` + `#[handler]` + jinja templates + CSS themes (`default`, `mono`) |
| Plumbing | `ref-list`, `cat-object`, `config get` | `command_passthrough` — the handler writes its own bytes, so `--output`, themes and the pager structurally cannot reach them |

Supporting modules: `repo.rs` (frozen state as consts), `config.rs` (walk-up `.gitlike.toml` → `$GITLIKE_CONFIG_HOME`/`$HOME` config, per-key precedence, both TOML spellings), `pager.rs`, `main.rs`.

## Two design decisions worth flagging

**`run_with` instead of `run`.** The framework only pages help and topics — there is no seam for paging command output, and `run()` owns the final write. So `main` takes the capture path and performs the process edge itself (one trailing newline via `writeln!`, stderr split, framework exit status), routing porcelain text through the pager.

**`ExternalFailure` instead of `AppFailure`.** `docs/topics/error-handling.md` and the handler contract both document `standout::cli::AppFailure` with worked examples; it does not exist in 9.0.0 under any path, and rustc offers no near-name suggestion. `ExternalFailure` has the same shape (nonzero status + verbatim stderr, no framing) and is what carries exit 3 and exit 1.

## Verified by running the binary

All four command outputs byte-for-byte (`od -c`); exit codes 0/1/2/3 including `config get`'s silence-on-both-streams; `--limit` overriding config; config precedence at two `.gitlike.toml` depths plus both user-config paths; plumbing byte-stability across all 8 `--output` modes × 5 environments.

**One gap:** this sandbox has no pty devices (`script` → "openpty: Operation not permitted", Python → "out of pty devices"), so I could not run with a real terminal on stdout. I exercised the paging machinery by temporarily forcing the terminal check to pass — pager selection, `GITLIKE_PAGER` over `PAGER`, blank values, `--no-pager` in both positions, plumbing refusing to page, fallback — then removed the override. The `is_terminal()` gate itself, and the framework-owned `auto`→`term`/`NO_COLOR` resolution, are unverified end-to-end.
